INTRODUCTION
At a glance
OUR YEAR IN BRIEF
-   We made clear progress implementing our refreshed strategy

-   We recorded profit for the period of 157.7 million EUR (2024: 202.2 million EUR), and generated a Return on Equity of 8.6%

-   We grew lending by 9.1% and deposits by 1.4%, and maintained lending quality, with Stage 3 loans at 2.0% of gross lending

-   Our liquidity and capital ratios remained strong with an LCR of 174.6%, MREL of 35.54%, and CET1 of 20.2% at year end

-   Karl von Rohr was appointed Chairman of the Supervisory Council effective 1 January 2026

ABOUT US
Luminor is the leading independent bank in the Baltics and the third-largest provider of financial services in our region. We
serve the financial needs of individuals, families, and companies. We are here to improve the financial health of our customers
and our home countries, and to support their growth. Further information about us can be found at www.luminor.ee.

We generated a profit for the period of 157.7 million EUR as compared to 202.2 million EUR in 2024. Total operating income
decreased by 95.6 million EUR due, in the main, to a decrease in Net interest income, as reference rates fell, while Total
operating expenses were unchanged. We recorded a slightly higher reversal of 1.9 million EUR in Expected credit losses,
supported by the positive macro environment and our recovery activities. We incurred no Bank taxes and resolution fee as
compared to a cost of 33.4 million EUR, as most sector-specific taxes lapsed, while income tax expense decreased by 17.1 million
EUR as Profit before tax reduced. We recorded a net interest margin of 2.71% and a cost to income ratio of 64.2%, and generated
a return on equity of 8.6%, or 11.9% assuming a CET1 ratio consistent with our target of 15%.

Loans to customers increased by 956.0 million EUR to 11.5 billion EUR. An increase of 589.1 million EUR in lending to individuals,
driven principally by growth in mortgage lending, was complemented by broad-based growth in loans to companies of 366.9
million EUR. We maintained the quality of our loan book. Stage 2 and 3 loans reduced by 153.6 million EUR driven in the main by
improvements in portfolio quality offset, in part, by a single exposure and revision of unlikely-to-pay criteria for individuals. At
year end the amount of Stage 3 loans was 231.9 million EUR, 2.0% of gross loans, or 168.5 million EUR after credit loss allowances,
against which we held collateral of 212.2 million EUR.

Our liquidity and capital positions are strong. At year end our Liquidity Coverage ratio was 174.6%, MREL was 35.54% and
Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio, including retained profit, was 20.2%, over 700 basis points above our CET1
requirements and Pillar 2 guidance of 13.13%. Our Tier 1 and Total capital ratios were boosted by our inaugural hybrid capital
issue, a 150 million EUR, perpetual Additional Tier 1 note. We propose to pay, in March, a dividend of 74.0 million EUR, or 50%
of the profit for the year attributable to the shareholder, as per our dividend policy.

We strengthened our governance with the appointment to the Supervisory Council of two new independent members, Karl von
Rohr, as Chairman, effective 1 January 2026 in succession to Nils Melngailis, and Peter Kleinschmidt as a member of the Council
and Chair of its Audit committee. The Management Board was enhanced with two new appointments to lead Retail Banking.
Jonna Pechter joined as Chief Marketing Officer, and Tanel Rebane was promoted to Chief Sales Officer. Their appointments
means both of our customer segments are headed by local business leaders.

The outlook for the Baltic region is positive. We look forward with confidence, despite the economic environment, because of
our belief in our home markets, our refreshed strategy, and our value proposition; we are here to improve the financial health
of our customers and our home countries, and to support their growth. In so doing, we will maintain our strong financial standing,
exercise prudent risk management, and fulfil our wider obligations. I look forward to sharing our progress.

We are Luminor
We are the leading independent bank in the Baltics and the third-largest provider of financial services in our region. We serve
the financial needs of individuals, families, and companies. We are here to improve the financial health of our customers and
our home countries, and to support their growth. Our name is formed from a blend of light, (lumin) to illuminate the way forward,
and nor, which reflects the Nordic roots of our founding banks.

Since re-dependence in the early 1990’s, the Baltic countries have transformed from planned economies to robust
democracies. All three countries are members of NATO, the European Union, and the Schengen Area, and have adopted the
euro. GDP per head has more than doubled since 2000, yet remains a fraction of the EU average. Governments have pursued
conservative fiscal policies and have Government debt to GDP ratios of below 40%, less than half the EU average. Principal
export markets are the other EU member countries, the United States, and the United Kingdom.

The total population of the three countries, at just over 6 million, is similar to other Nordic countries such as Denmark, Finland
or Norway. Like their neighbours, the Baltic countries score highly for openness and freedom. In Transparency International’s
2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, all the Baltic countries were ranked in the top quartile of 181 countries globally, with an
average score of 67, higher than France, Spain, or Italy, and well ahead of countries in the CEE region.

The Baltic banking market is competitive but profitable. We compete against two Swedish banks which operate across the
region, together with smaller scale, local banks in each country. Lending balances in the region have grown in recent years, but
low private indebtedness, including low mortgage penetration, gives room for further credit growth.

We were created in 2017 when DNB and Nordea joined their Baltic operations. We manage our business by customer segment
– Retail Banking and Corporate Banking – on a pan-Baltic basis from our headquarters in Estonia and branches in Latvia and
Lithuania. Deposits from customers, and customer investments, are protected by Tagatisfond, the Estonian Guarantee Fund.
Our subsidiaries provide leasing, manage pension funds and offer e-commerce payments.

Retail Banking provides banking services to individuals and micro-businesses, and is responsible for our pension management
companies. Corporate Banking provides banking services to legal entities and is responsible for our leasing and e-commerce
payments companies. We operate only in the Baltic countries and target our services at residents of the Baltic countries, or
individuals and companies with a strong connection to the Baltic countries.

We are owned, via Luminor Holding, by a consortium led by private equity funds managed by Blackstone (80.05%) and DNB Bank
(19.95%). We are regulated by the European Central Bank (the ECB), have a well-developed governance structure and aspire to
the highest standards of conduct. Our non-executive Supervisory Council oversees the executive Management Board. The
Supervisory Council members are appointed either from amongst the nominees of the shareholders of Luminor Holding, or are
independent. The executive Management Board members are a blend of local and international executives.

We organise our control framework across three lines. The first line, our two banking divisions and three support divisions –
Finance, Operations, and Technology – are responsible for managing their risks according to our policies, procedures and
controls. The second line is a control function comprised of our Compliance and Risk divisions which are independent of, and
monitor the activities of, the first line. Internal Audit serves as the third line which assesses the effectiveness of the first two
lines. We do not tolerate financial crime. To prevent, detect, and report any potential financial crime, we have a low-risk
appetite, have built our compliance culture, and enhanced our risk management capabilities. We work closely with governments
and supervisors and use this work to augment our systems and processes, to raise our effectiveness.

We are well placed to grow with our customers. We have a simple and straightforward business model; we are a retail and
corporate bank, and our business is balanced, by customer type, by sources and uses of funds, and by country. We are easy to
understand: Loans to customers’ account for two-thirds of our assets; we are funded primarily with Deposits from customers;
and, we are well capitalised. We will continue to support the development of Baltic capital markets, and are committed to
carbon neutrality by 2050.

We have good market shares in anchor products, such as residential mortgages, and
lending for larger corporates, where we will maintain our strong position. In Retail
                                                                                          Chief Executive
Banking, we will develop our daily banking offering to increase our number of primary
bank relationships, maximise our share of current accounts, and grow fee income. We will also grow consumer lending on the
back of our end-to-end digital offering. In Corporate Banking, we will capitalise on our existing platform to accelerate growth
in lending to SME customers. Together these actions will increase our share of significant Baltic banking revenue pools.

We have already transformed our IT systems. Our next step is to improve the efficiency of our IT systems and digitise our
operating model. Therefore, we will migrate our three existing, country-based legacy systems, operating on-premises, to a
single, modern, cloud-based, pan-Baltic platform. This migration will align our IT systems with our pan-Baltic operating, legal,
and regulatory model; increase automation, and hence customer satisfaction, and lower unit costs; and improve the pace of IT
developments and build scalability. These enhancements will optimise customer on-boarding and service, support ‘compliance
by design’, and intensify cybersecurity.

To remain compliant with changing regulations we will continue to develop our compliance culture, including adherence to the
highest ethical and conduct standards, and so build sustainable compliance into a competitive advantage, including ESG. We
believe a strong compliance culture creates trust between our stakeholders and us, and so supports a sustainable business
model. Our compliance culture has four pillars: employees behave with integrity; business and control divisions work as partners;
we are open and reliable with our stakeholders; and we are engaged with current requirements and anticipate new expectations.
We are committed to meeting our Sustainability targets, aligned with becoming carbon neutral by 2050.

Our plans are ambitious, but I am confident we will achieve them, given our good market positions, the team we have in place,
and examples of early successes. Our business model is straight-forward and our balance sheet is robust with undoubted
strengths in capital and liquidity, asset quality and risk management; we are already a safe home for customers’ deposits, and
our loan portfolio is well diversified; and we have a unique regional presence, with strong brand recognition, and high customer
satisfaction. Over the past year we have appointed new heads of our two customer segments. They, together with existing
Management Board members, each of whom have a pedigree of delivering change effectively, have demonstrated already some
early strategic ‘wins’.

As we implement our strategy, I will provide updates on our developments. As a Management Board we are accountable for our
improvements, will celebrate our successes, and be candid where we need to do better. I look forward to sharing our progress
as my colleagues and I, through our home markets of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, make Luminor an undoubted top 3 universal
pan-Baltic bank by end 2027.

In the commentary below we compare the result for the year to the prior year

We generated a profit of 157.7 million EUR as compared to 202.2 million EUR. A decrease of 95.6 million EUR in Total operating
income, due mainly to a decrease in Net interest income, and unchanged Total operating expenses, was offset in part by an
increased reversal of Expected credit losses, the elimination of Bank taxes and resolution fee, and lower Income tax expense,
which resulted in a 44.5 million EUR, or 22.0% decrease in Profit for the period. We generated a return on equity of 8.6%.

Total operating income of 537.2 million EUR decreased 15.1%. Net interest income decreased by 87.9 million EUR, or 17.3%,
driven, chiefly, by reduced deposit margins as reference rates fell. In addition, lending spreads decreased due to competitive
pressures on new lending and changes in mortgage refinancing regulations which resulted in increasing demand for repricing
of existing loans. The impact of these effects was offset in part by growth in lending balances and supported by a decrease in
overall funding expenses including a reduction in the amount of covered bonds in issue for half of the year. We generated a net
interest margin of 2.71%, as compared to 3.33%. Net fee and commission income decreased by 4.2 million EUR, or 4.7%, as a
Pension performance fee generated last year did not recur. Net other operating income decreased by 3.5 million EUR, or 9.9%,
driven, in the main, by lower Net gain from financial items, as a legacy bond portfolio managed by Treasury, designated at fair
value, reduced in size and income from foreign exchange transactions decreased.

Total operating expenses of 345.0 million EUR were unchanged. An increase in Personnel expenses of 6.2 million EUR, or 4.2%,
as we insourced critical functions, was more than offset by a reduction of 8.8 million EUR, or 5.0%, in Other administration
expenses as we lowered Consultancy and professional services spending by 6.6 million EUR and IT-related expense by 1.3 million
EUR. Depreciation, amortisation, and impairment expense decreased by 1.1 million EUR, or 5.4%, as we wrote down 9.7 million
EUR of goodwill associated with the purchase of Maksekeskus as compared to a write-down of 11.1 million EUR, and Loss on
derecognition of non-financial assets increased by 3.7 million EUR, as we realised a higher loss on derecognition of capitalised
software costs. Reflecting the movements above, the cost/ income ratio increased by 9.7%-points to 64.2%.

We recorded a reversal of 1.9 million EUR in Expected credit losses as compared to a reversal of 1.3 million EUR. The reversals
were driven mostly by the positive macro environment that has contributed to low level of new defaults. In addition, successful
restructuring and recovery activities led to reversals of previously established loan loss provisions. We incurred no Bank taxes
and resolution fee in 2025 as compared to a cost of 33.4 million EUR, as most sector-specific taxes lapsed and we mitigated the
effect of the second Latvian bank tax as we grew our customer balances. Income tax expense of 36.4 million EUR, an effective
tax rate of 18.6%, as compared to 20.9%, decreased by 17.1 million EUR, or nearly a third, as Profit before tax reduced and due
to changes in deferred tax assets and liabilities. Profit attributable to our shareholder was 147.9 million EUR as compared to
202.2 million EUR.

In the commentaries below we compare the year-end balance sheet to the balance sheet at the end of the prior year

In 2025 we increased Loans to customers by 956.0 million EUR and grew Deposits from customers by 158.0 million EUR. The
total balance sheet increased by 178.3 million EUR to 15.9 billion EUR, as increased lending was offset by a decrease of 1,168.7
million EUR in Cash and balances with central banks while Debt securities increased by 422.1 million EUR. Loans to customers
accounted for over seventy percent of total assets, funded wholly by deposits.

Loans to customers increased by 9.1% to 11.5 billion EUR. An increase of 589.1 million EUR in lending to individuals, driven
principally by growth in mortgage loans, was complemented by growth in loans to businesses of 264.3 million EUR driven by
broad-based growth in lending including to the Utilities, Real Estate, and Wholesale & retail sectors, offset in part by a reduction
in lending to Construction, and Other, sectors. Loans to Financial institutions grew by 20.6 million EUR and loans to the Public
sector by 82.0 million EUR.

Cash and balances with central banks decreased by over a third and Debt securities increased by a quarter as we reshaped our
excess resources. Our liquidity portfolio consists, in the main, of high-quality government and covered bonds which can be
pledged with the European Central Bank to allow us to obtain additional liquidity.

Deposits from customers increased by 1.4% as we balanced our liabilities and adjusted our deposit rates selectively. An increase
in deposit balances from Individuals, Financial institutions, and Public sector customers was offset in part by a managed
decrease in deposits from Businesses. Demand deposits decreased by 105.2 million EUR while Term deposits increased by 263.2
million EUR. At year end, Term deposits accounted for a quarter of Deposits from customers. Debt securities issued decreased
by 72.5 million EUR as we lowered the amount of senior bonds issued.

Equity increased by 198.6 million EUR as we issued our inaugural Additional Tier I security in 2025, a 150 million EUR perpetual
obligation, and retained the Profit for the period. These additions were offset by payment of a 101.1 million EUR dividend for
2024.

Our own funds and MREL-eligible instruments totalled 35.54% of Total Risk Exposure Amount (TREA) and 16.82% of our Leverage
Ratio Exposure (LRE). With effect from 1 January 2026 our MREL targets were confirmed at 23.69% of TREA plus combined
buffer requirement, down from 23.77% previously, and 5.91% of LRE.

Our Liquidity Coverage ratio decreased by 30.5%-points to 174.6% as we increased Loans to customers and paid a dividend for
2024. Our Net Stable Funding ratio was 134.1%, a decrease of 9.5%-points. Available stable funding increased, driven by issuance
of our AT1 security and by a higher amount of Debt securities issued with remaining maturities greater than one year. Required
stable funding also increased, driven in the main by the increase in Loans to customers. Both ratios remained well above the
100% minima.

We are strongly capitalised, with own funds at 31 December of over 1.9 billion EUR. Measured on our ‘Management view’, which
includes profit for the period which we will retain, our Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1), Tier 1, and Total capital ratios were above
20.0% at year end. As reported on a regulatory basis, pending ECB approval of year end audited profits, the ratios were 19.2%,
21.0%, and 23.6%, respectively. Our target CET1 capital ratio is 15.0%.

We have initiated the final part of our capital efficiency programme, to return excess equity capital to our shareholder – subject
to regulatory approval. Furthermore, we will maintain the efficiency of our capital resources, maximising the amount of issued
capital consistent with our capital requirements. In the meantime, we continue to assess the opportunity to issue senior non-
preferred debt as we anticipate possible changes in deposit preference regulations to maintain our current A2 rating.

Our CET1 ratio increased by 0.1%-points, with similar rates of growth in both Equity capital and Risk exposure amounts. Our Tier
1 and Total capital ratios increased by 2.0%-points and by 1.9%-points respectively, after we issued our inaugural Additional
Tier 1 capital security, a 150 million EUR, perpetual subordinated note, resettable six and a half years after issuance. The security
was issued to Luminor Holding, our parent company, which, in turn, sold a similar security, rated Ba2 by Moody’s, to investors.

Risk exposure amounts increased by 324.8 million EUR, or 4.3%. Credit risk exposure amounts, which we measure on a
standardised basis, grew 631.5 million EUR, or 9.8%, as we increased Loans to customers, and completed a year-long, in-depth
review of our credit risk exposure calculation methodologies and processes, offset in part by our adoption of the requirements
of Basel IV in January 2025. The same requirements drove a reduction of 289.4 million EUR, or just over a quarter, in Operational
risk exposure amounts, as per the standardised measurement approach, while Other risk exposure amounts decreased by 17.3
million, or over half, driven, in the main, by decreased market risk exposure as we revised our calculation methodology.

Our capital ratios remain well above our minima which, at 31 December 2025, require us to have a CET1 ratio exceeding 11.63%,
a Tier 1 ratio above 13.60% and a Total Capital ratio greater than 16.23%. Since June 2025 these minima include an additional
countercyclical buffer of 0.5% of our risk exposures in Latvia, which increased the minimum capital amount by 14 basis points.
Our capital targets and internal limits are set at the regulatory expectation (including Pillar 2 Guidance of 1.5%) plus a
Management Buffer. Our leverage ratio increased by 0.9%-points as Tier 1 capital grew by more than Leverage ratio exposure
amounts, as compared to the required minimum ratio of 3.0%.

borrower, a 400 million EUR Green Bond issued by one of the leading green energy producers in the Baltic region, a 70 million
EUR bond issued by a development financial institution, as well as a series of securities issued by real estate companies.

ECONOMIC ENVIRONMENT

a. Year-on-year change, Data as at 27 January 2026


The economy of the European Union continued to grow through 2025, albeit at an uneven pace across countries and sectors,
with Spain the powerhouse for growth while Germany underperformed. The economies of the Nordic countries did better than
in the prior year, with expansion in Sweden offsetting lower growth in Finland, where weaknesses in in the real estate and
construction sectors were observed. Money market interest rates declined and stabilised slightly above 2%. Lower interest
rates supported the improved performance of the Baltic economies directly as interest on most household mortgages and
business loans is set at a spread to short-term money market rates. Growth prospects for the year 2026 remain stable, aided
by diminished perceptions of geopolitical risks.

Economic growth converged across the Baltic states as compared to the prior year, with Estonia and Latvia returning to growth
alongside Lithuania. Expansion of the Estonian economy was aided by energy and manufacturing sectors, though the relatively
weak Nordic real estate and construction markets continues to have a negative impact, while Latvian numbers being boosted
by strong manufacturing and export sectors, and Lithuania benefitted from close relationships with the strongly growing Polish
economy.

Inflation rates remained above the euro area levels in all Baltic states. Estonian inflation was higher because of increase in the
value added tax from 22% to 24% in July 2025, introduction of car tax and several other administrative measures leading to
price level increases. The inflation rates in Latvia (3.7%) and Lithuania (3.8%) show the wage pressure coming from real wage
growth following the previous decrease in real wages and strong domestic demand. Food prices were increased inflation while
the strong euro and cheap Chinese imports provided a countervailing push downwards in prices.

Unemployment rates remained somewhat elevated compared to European levels as the statistics reflect higher unemployment
rates following inclusion of refugees from the war in Ukraine. That said, employment levels remain very close to historic peak
levels. Wages continue to increase. Nominal wages continued to grow, with growth of around 8% in both Latvia and Lithuania in
the third quarter of 2025. Estonian wage growth slowed to 5.7%, but with the increase of the personal income tax in 2024 and
elevated inflation rates, real wages fell. Latvian and Lithuanian purchasing power of wages now exceeds clearly the previous
peak level of 2021 as wage growth has exceeded inflation for some time.

Governments in all the Baltic states run budget deficits and are offering support to their respective economies. With the debt-
to-GDP ratios among the lowest in the European Union, there is ample room to provide additional support to the economies
whenever necessary. Deficits have had limited effects on the debt-to-GDP ratios as nominal GDP has been growing fast. The
outlook for all the Baltic countries remains optimistic for 2026 with incomes increasing, stable interest rates at prevailing lower
levels, and continued expansion of the European Union economy.

BUSINESS DEVELOPMENTS
We refreshed our strategy, as per ‘Our strategy’ section, above. In summary, we intend to strengthen further our position as a
top 3, universal, pan-Baltic bank by end of 2027, with a digital-first operating model, demonstrated track record, and a modern
and scalable IT platform. To realise our ambition, we are focused on three areas: first, to grow our customer franchise; second,
to improve the efficiency of our IT systems and digitalise our operating model; and third, to remain compliant with changing
regulations.

Through the year we continued to improve the experience of our customers banking with us, and are taking steps to accelerate
these enhancements further in the period ahead. We strengthened our security and regulatory compliance processes and
systems and, as well, maintained our focus on compliance with the Digital Operational Resilience Act.

To support the growth and development of medium-sized companies in the Baltic region, assets managed by our pension fund
management subsidiaries committed to invest over 25.0 million EUR in a new private equity and debt funds, which will invest
majority of its assets in the region.

We made several changes to the Supervisory Council and its committees. Karl von Rohr was appointed Chairman of the Council
effective 1 January 2026 succeeding Nils Melngailis. Karl brings three decades of international banking experience gained at
Deutsche Bank, where he served as a member of the Management Board, President of the Management Board and Chief
Executive of Deutsche Bank’s Private Bank, and Chairman of the Supervisory Board of DWS Group. Nils will remain a member
of the Council and was appointed, for 2026, Senior Advisor.

Peter Kleinschmidt was appointed as member of the Council. He is a former Partner at PwC and has three decades experience
in financial services, governance, and compliance, with expertise in auditing, risk management, and digital transformation. Since
2023, Peter has focused on investment and advisory roles. From 2024 until March 2026, he was a member of the supervisory
board and the Chairman of the Risk & Audit committee of N26, the German neobank. Peter is Chairman of the Council’s Audit
committee, and a member of the Risk committee. The appointments, above, are subject to regulatory approval.

Maria Elena Cappello, Mathias Favetto, and Betsy Nelson were re-elected as members of the Council for new terms of five years
each. Sandy Kinney Pritchard stepped down from the Council and its Audit and Risk committees, after which Bjoern Erik Naess
chaired the Audit committee on an interim basis before the appointment of Peter Kleinschmidt.

The Management Board was strengthened with two new appointments to lead Retail Banking. Jonna Pechter joined as Chief
Marketing Officer, with responsibility for retail products, marketing, and branding, and Tanel Rebane was appointed as Chief
Sales Officer, accountable for retail sales, customer service touchpoints, private banking, and our pension subsidiaries. Jonna
has over two decades of experience in retail banking and product management in the Baltic counties, especially Estonia while
Tanel has worked for us since 2020 leading customer relations, sales, and innovation. Together they are accountable for
improving the performance of Retail banking. Following these appointments, we reorganised the operations of Retail banking.

We simplified the structure of our IT organisation, and embedded an engineering first, distributed way of working that supports
better our focus on customers and business development. We also prepared implementation of key deliverables of the Instant
Payments Act. We insourced critical functions and terminated our outsourcing contract with Kyndryl. In addition, we launched
the Verification of Payee service to help make instant payments safer and reduce the risk of fraud and misdirected payments.

We completed the purchase of the outstanding minority interest in Maksekeskus, our e-commerce payments subsidiary,
recorded a small gain on sale as we sold the shares we owned in our Associate, Kredītinformācijas birojs AS, and completed the
liquidation of SIA Promano Lat, our subsidiary.

We continued to work closely with our regulators. Finantsinspektsioon issued a precept in September about customer
notifications and internal procedures for terminating or refusing basic payment service agreements. We adjusted our
procedures to align them with the supervisor’s observations.

PREVENTING FINANCIAL CRIME
We do not tolerate financial crime, and we remain committed to maintaining our strong conduct, ethics, and risk culture. We
market our products and services only to residents of the Baltic countries, and to individuals and companies with a strong
connection to those countries.

Our commitment to protecting our customers and preserving the integrity of the financial system remains at the heart of our
actions. We work closely with regulatory and supervisory authorities and use this work to enhance our systems and processes.
We are committed to following all laws and regulations, standards, guidelines, and recommendations.

We continued to improve our organisational setup, governance, and processes throughout the year to ensure that our activities
are aligned with our risk appetite and our risk-based approach, while keeping a clear focus on the experience for our customers.
We consolidated our efforts to prevent financial crime and strengthened the operational structures supporting them.

We remain committed to the protection of human rights and to countering the financing of terrorism and the proliferation of
weapons of mass destruction. We report possible sanctions breaches and violations to the regulatory authorities.

We advanced our anti-money laundering (AML) capabilities, sanctions compliance measures, and anti-fraud framework through
ongoing development and iterative deliveries. We continued to prioritise and enhance our risk management measures for
tackling fraud. These efforts included continuous technological upgrades, the application of risk mitigation strategies, and
regular training for our staff so they can address fraudulent activities more effectively. Our focus during the whole year remained
on strengthening both the efficiency and the effectiveness of our fraud prevention framework.

Over the year we continued to enhance our risk culture and carried out a range of awareness-raising activities. We organised
63 training courses on compliance risk for a total of over 30,000 hours during the year. We ran several internal communication
and engagement projects to promote discussion and a common understanding around different aspects of risk culture, we
introduced a user-friendly Code of Conduct Employee Guide, and we organised a dedicated Conduct Month.

We took proactive steps to make our customers more aware about fraud. We ran communication initiatives throughout the
year to empower customers and the wider public with the knowledge and skills they need to recognise possible attempts at
fraud in a climate where criminal activity is always evolving fast.

We remain dedicated to staying at the forefront of technological advances and to refining our risk management measures for
fraud risk to adapt to emerging threats and ensure the continued security of the financial assets of our customers.

EVENTS AFTER PERIOD END
On 27 January 2026 we announced the redemption of our 500 million SEK floating rate senior notes, due March 2027. The notes
will be redeemed on 27 March 2026, the optional redemption date, at 100% of their nominal amount, together with accrued but
unpaid interest. The listing of the notes on the Irish Stock Exchange will be cancelled thereafter.

GENERAL INFORMATION
We have prepared this sustainability statement in accordance with the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) as
transposed into Estonian law, and the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS).This statement is based on the Double
Materiality Assessment (DMA) of potentially material ESG matters, and the resulting definition of the related impacts, risks and
opportunities of the material topics, and has sections aligned with ESRS guidelines; General, Environmental, Social and
Governance information. The scope of the consolidation is the same as for our financial statement.

In addition, we include non-CSRD mandated metrics relevant to our strategy. See Note 5, CSRD content index, Note 6,
Datapoints that derive from other EU legislation, and Note 7, Datapoints from other legislation or sustainability standards, below.

Many of the climate-related quantitative disclosures for our portfolio that are covered in this sustainability statement are
compiled on a best effort basis and are based on proxy methodologies to some extent. These include the reported Scope 1, 2
and 3 emissions and EPC reports. The main sources of estimation and the outcome uncertainty for the metrics disclosed are
provided in the sections 'Environmental information' and 'Notes to the sustainability statement'. The two main sources of
measurement uncertainty arise because of our use of industry, not company specific, data and proxy data, based on building
type, location, and year of construction.

Our DMA process, which includes our suppliers and customers, identifies the concerns of stakeholders, informs our decision-
making and guides our disclosures. For our 2025 Assessment we updated our methodology, garnered the views of our
stakeholders and reviewed publications. From these we concluded impacts, risks, and opportunities over the three-time
horizons consistent with regulatory requirements and the financial sector practice. We made four principal changes to this
year’s assessment as compared to the prior year, as per section 'Changes' below.

We have not omitted any specific piece of information corresponding to intellectual property, know-how or the results of
innovation, nor have we used the exemption from disclosing impending developments or matters that are under negotiation.
No exemption has been applied, except for sensitive matters which are indicated in Context index. We have not used any
external body other than the assurance provider to evaluate the metrics in the Sustainability Statement.

To support our DMA, we engaged with stakeholders using surveys, focus groups, and analysis of publicly available disclosures.
While indirect data sources such as annual reports provided valuable insights, we acknowledge that metrics derived from these
sources carry inherent limitations in accuracy due to subjectivity, representativeness, and standardisation challenges.
Nonetheless, these inputs enabled us to identify and validate key Impacts, Risks and Opportunities (IRO) and enhance the
reliability of our ESG risk metrics across the value chain. To improve the accuracy of value chain metrics derived from indirect
sources, we plan to expand supplier and customer engagement through standardised surveys and internal scenario-based
assessments aligned with evolving science and our updated Climate and Environment Transition Plan. In addition, to reduce our
dependency on metrics derived from indirect sources we plan to increase the share of customer reported data.

Double Materiality Assessment and Sustainability Reporting Processes
Our annual Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) identifies the concerns of stakeholders, informs our decision-making and
guides our disclosures.

In 2025, we completed our fifth DMA based on an updated methodology leading to a more focused set of material topics, which
affirmed Climate change, Biodiversity and ecosystem, and Consumers and end-users as material topics while excluding other
topics that no longer meet the revised disclosure criteria. Topics that were considered material in the previous reporting period
but are no longer classified as such under the 2025 DMA have been excluded from this year’s reporting scope.

Our governance framework ensures compliance with applicable laws and regulations through policies, mandatory training, and
channels for whistleblowing and speak-up. These measures safeguard trust and accountability across our operations. In
addition, for topics that are no longer material, we have reviewed the targets, plans, and progress disclosed in our previous
sustainability report and provided updates in the relevant chapters of the statement, under 'Progress and updates since last
report' sections to maintain transparency and continuity.

Our DMA identifies adverse impacts using an impact‑based assessment aligned with ESRS and assesses sustainability‑related
risks and opportunities separately using ESRS financial materiality criteria. In 2025, we prioritised activities and relationships in
high-risk sectors - such as agriculture, energy, and manufacturing - based on portfolio exposure and external benchmarks. In
our assessment, we focused on Baltic countries for environmental and social risks, and business relationships with suppliers
and customers whose ESG practices may pose reputational or operational risks.

To understand how our activities may impact affected stakeholders, we consult stakeholder using surveys and focus groups to
gather their perspectives on environmental and social risks. These insights were integrated into our assessment and
prioritisation of material topics. Our time horizons differ from those defined in ESRS due to regulatory requirements—such as
ECB climate risk assessment timelines—and the financial planning and business cycle characteristics of the financial sector.
Accordingly, we use: short-term (up to 3 years), medium-term (4–9 years), and long-term (beyond 10 years, aligned with our
2050 climate targets).

CHANGE TO THE PROCESS FROM THE PREVIOUS REPORTING PERIOD
Material information on impacts, risks, and opportunities is determined based on the double materiality principles outlined in
the ESRS and aligned with our corporate strategy and stakeholder priorities.

During the reporting period, we enhanced our process for identifying, assessing, and managing IROs. We introduced new
materiality thresholds, including a secondary financial materiality threshold for non-financial risks, aligned with ESRS, to better
reflect the information needs of our primary report users. Our methodology was refined through updated assessment scales
for impact dimensions and non-financial opportunities, the adoption of quantification templates aligned with our risk and
performance management frameworks, and the alignment of financial risk thresholds to our Risk Policy. In addition, we
introduced a financial materiality threshold for opportunities and further integrated the DMA into our risk and overall
management processes.




22     Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025

=== pdf p.23 ===
Identifying material matters and IROs
PROCESS
Our Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) applies a structured methodology to identify, assess, and prioritise Impacts, Risks,
and Opportunities (IROs) across our value chain. First, we conduct a gap analysis of the previous year’s IRO list and analysis of
internal and external sources. We identify our positive and negative actual and potential impacts, and the connected risks and
opportunities, followed by an assessment using updated materiality thresholds. The thresholds are defined in our Double
Materiality Assessment Procedure, Risk Policy and Performance Management Procedure, we use a combination of internal
expertise and external benchmarks - including Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB) Materiality Map, peer
disclosures, and professional publications - to ensure completeness and relevance.

To ensure that our IRO identification process is evidence-based, forward-looking, and aligned with ESRS and financial sector
expectations we apply assumptions with regard to time horizon definitions and the related forward-looking subjective
assessments; sector prioritisation based on portfolio exposure and regulatory relevance; stakeholder input about material
concerns; and indirect data sources.

We apply predefined qualitative and quantitative input parameters to systematically identify and assess material impacts, risks
and opportunities: including internal and external data sources, stakeholder inputs. Impact materiality is assessed using scale,
scope and (for negative impacts) irremediable character (severity), and likelihood only for potential impacts. Financial materiality
for risks and opportunities is assessed separately using likelihood of occurrence and defined financial thresholds linked to
potential magnitude of effects. time horizons tailored to the financial sector, sectoral exposure and climate/environmental risk
levels, stakeholder relevance, and applicability across subsidiaries.

Our DMA considers impacts arising both from our own operations and through business relationships across the value chain.
Engagement with external stakeholders further informs our understanding of indirect impacts, enabling a comprehensive view
of our footprint and responsibilities.

Impacts linked to suppliers, customers, and other partners are assessed by subject matter experts who review due diligence
outcomes, including ESG governance, controversies, and sector-specific risks. These experts also contribute to the design of
due diligence tools, ensuring that high-risk relationships are flagged and reflected in the IRO prioritisation.

ASSESSMENT METHODOLOGY
To quantify financial risks and opportunities, we applied methods aligned with our internal performance and risk management
frameworks. Financial risks and opportunities were assessed based on the potential magnitude of the financial effects and
likelihood. Financial opportunities were assessed using bespoke templates integrated into our performance management
system, while financial risks were evaluated using two distinct templates - one for credit risk and another for non-credit financial
risks - aligned with our enterprise risk management framework.

Non-Financial risks were assessed based on Luminor internal non-financial risk grid covering customer, regulatory, reputational,
and operational dimensions. Non-financial risks were assessed based on their potential magnitude of effects and likelihood.
Non-financial opportunities were assessed applying a custom 0-5 opportunities' potential significance assessment scales and
likelihood applied across the three time horizons.

Actual negative impacts were assessed based on severity, and potential negative impacts were assessed based on severity and
likelihood, with severity taking precedence for human rights impacts. Positive impacts were assessed based on scale and scope
for actual impacts, and scale, scope and likelihood for potential impacts. Impact materiality and financial materiality were
assessed using distinct ESRS criteria. Likelihood is assessed for potential impacts, risks and opportunities. For actual impacts,
likelihood is not applicable, and assessment is based on the relevant impact criteria only. Likelihood is assessed using our
internal non-financial risk grid as defined in our Risk Policy.

We prioritise actual negative impacts based on their severity, considering scale, scope, irremediable character. Potential
negative impacts are prioritized based on severity and likelihood, using custom scales and thresholds across the three time
horizons. Positive impacts are assessed based on their significance, determined by scale and scope for actual impacts, and by




                                                                                        Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025          23

=== pdf p.24 ===
scale, scope and likelihood for potential impacts. Impacts are evaluated using structured scoring and prioritised against defined
materiality thresholds to determine which sustainability matters are material for reporting.

Sustainability-related financial risks are prioritised using the same materiality thresholds as other financial risks, in line with our
Risk Policy. For non-financial risks, an additional financial materiality threshold is applied to identify disclosure-relevant risks,
considering potential impacts such as loss of customers or deposits, and effects on net commission income (NCI), net interest
income (NII), or operating costs.

CONNECTION OF IMPACTS WITH RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES
We identified impacts through our DMA, then connected relevant risks and opportunities from previous assessments and
identified additional ones based on internal and external data analysis, focus group discussions, and stakeholder engagement.

DECISION-MAKING PROCESS AND RELATED INTERNAL CONTROL PROCEDURES
The outcome of our DMA is validated through a structured governance process. Assessments are performed by subject matter
experts, signed off by Level 2 IRO owners, and reviewed by second-line controllers based on risk type mapping to our Risk
Policy. Final approval is granted by our management bodies.

INTEGRATION OF DOUBLE MATERIALITY ASSESSMENT INTO RISK AND OVERALL MANAGEMENT PROCESSES
We embed the DMA in our risk management framework through a multi-layered approach which draws on outputs from existing
internal risk assessments to align with our risk tolerance and strategic priorities. All identified sustainability-related risks are
mapped to our established risk taxonomy, to promote consistency and comparability across risk categories. A dedicated risk
controller validates these risks. Risk evaluations follow our internal policy, applying predefined thresholds and methodologies
to determine materiality and prioritisation. Identified sustainability-related risks are documented and managed in line with our
risk management framework.

For material ESG-related risks and related impacts, we developed transition plans that outline strategic responses, targets, and
implementation pathways. These plans are reviewed and approved by management board and are aligned with our long-term
business strategy and regulatory obligations. Progress against these plans is monitored and reported regularly by the designated
transition plan or risk owners.

Controls and procedures applied to manage IROs
We have established following controls and procedures to effectively manage impacts, risks, and opportunities:

Identification and assessment: we have a procedure in place, regulating roles and process of executing the annual double
materiality assessment and procedure for identification of climate-related and environmental risks, assessment of their impacts
and addressing them;

Oversight: The Council oversees the identification, assessment, and management of IROs and approves outcomes of double
materiality assessment. Board is responsible for approval of the outcome of the Analysis of Impact of Climate & Environmental
Risk Drivers on the Business Environment (C&E RBE); and integration into strategy and internal processes: the Board discusses
the outcomes of double materiality assessment and C&E RBE outcome. The Board also approves the transition plans to treat
the identified material risks and ensures monitoring and reporting of the progress of these plans.

The Board discussion of C&E RBE outcome aims to address the implication of the outcome on the business model and our
strategy. Considering that ESG risks are treated as risk drivers that can impact all other material risk types meaning they are
embedded within and managed through established risk management processes for overarching risk categories.




Risk management and internal controls over sustainability reporting
We updated our Sustainability Reporting Standard in 2025.

We use a three-step process of compilation, review, and approval, to prepare the IRO assessment and sustainability disclosures.
First, the business owners assign subject matter experts for each function or process, who then define the requirements for
specific inputs, and review the requirements for validity, verification and disclosure purposes with an eye to data availability and
strategic considerations. The qualitative and quantitative disclosures are then validated and approved. Second, the Head of the
Sustainability Department and Head of Investor Relations and Sustainable Finance confirm that all the signoffs have been
completed and sign off the statement themselves. Third and finally, the disclosures are attested by the CFO and CRO.

For risk assessment in scope of DMA, we used materiality thresholds as described above. All risks above the threshold are
considered material IROs for disclosure. To validate the risks identified for both qualitative and quantitative disclosures, we
apply several controls, such as the 'four eyes' principle and second line risk controller review and challenge. The qualitative data
we gather is validated by the business owner of the disclosure to ensure completeness and accuracy and that it is presented in
accordance with the applicable internal and external regulations. For quantitative disclosures on climate and environmental
data, we follow our Data Quality Management procedure and principles and the ESG Data Management Procedure.

The primary source for data collection is our data warehouses and, if unavailable, we aim to collect primary data directly from
customers or from external data sources. The data collected is then reported in aggregated form. For data that is not available,
data proxy methodologies based on international standards such as PCAF are used, or alternatives are developed in-house.
Once the data has been aggregated for specific reporting purposes, the content is validated by the data owners or service
owners. The four eyes principle is followed when the data is validated, as the data validator must then be someone other than
the data provider.

Strategy, business model and value chain
We are the leading independent bank in the Baltics and the third-largest provider of financial services in our region. We serve
the financial needs of individuals, families, and companies. We are here to improve the financial health of our customers and
our home countries, and to support their growth.

We were created in 2017 when DNB and Nordea joined their Baltic operations, to serve the financial needs of these dynamic
economies. We manage our business by customer segment – Retail Banking and Corporate Banking – on a pan-Baltic basis from
our headquarters in Estonia and branches in Latvia and Lithuania. Our subsidiaries provide leasing, manage pension funds and
offer e-commerce payments. Retail Banking provides banking services to individuals and micro-businesses and is responsible
for our pension companies. Corporate Banking provides banking services to legal entities and is responsible for our leasing and
e-commerce payments companies. We operate only in the Baltic countries and target our services at residents of the Baltic
countries, or individuals and companies with a strong connection to the Baltic countries.

We are well placed to grow with our customers. We have a simple and straightforward business model; we are a retail and
corporate bank, and our business is balanced, by customer type, by sources and uses of funds, and by country. We are easy to
understand Loans to customers’ account for two-thirds of our assets, we are funded primarily with Deposits from customers,
and are well capitalised. We support the development of Baltic capital markets and are committed to carbon neutrality by
2050.

Our upstream value chain network includes key partners such as investors, service providers like IT firms, regulatory bodies,
and other financial institutions.

Our business model resilience is ensured through our integrated strategy planning processes and our internal governance
framework. We organise our internal control framework aligned to the three lines of defence model. The first line is our business
and support divisions, which are responsible for managing their risks in accordance with our policies, procedures and controls.
The second line is a control function that comprises our compliance and risk divisions, which are independent of the first line,
and monitor its activities. Internal audit is the third line, and it assesses the effectiveness of the first two lines.

Our three-year financial plan is jointly developed by business and risk functions, aligned with our risk appetite and financial
targets, including climate targets, and is approved annually by the Council. Business model risks are continuously assessed
through market, geopolitical and performance analyses, with ESG, including climate and environmental considerations fully
embedded into planning.

Corporate Governance report
We have a two-tier governance structure where supervisory (non-executive) functions are carried out by the Supervisory
Council (‘Council') and management (executive) functions are carried out by the Management Board (‘Board’). The Council
oversees the activities of the Board in managing Luminor. Members of the Council cannot be at the same time members of the
Board. We refer to the Council and Board collectively as ‘Management Bodies’.

We are governed by Estonian Law and follow applicable legal regulations of the European Union and guidelines provided by the
European Banking Authority on internal governance. Aligned with these legal requirements and guidelines we have adopted
internal regulations to ensure robust governance. These include the implementation of the ‘three lines’ model, comprehensive
risk management process, defined internal values, conflict of interest management principles, compliance frameworks, regular
internal control mechanisms and remuneration policies. Our Governance Policy, our principal internal governance document,
defines and guides these practices. We updated our Governance Policy in October 2025.

The General Meeting of Shareholders (General Meeting) is a statutory body through which our shareholders exercise their rights.
We have one class of registered common shares. Each share grants one vote at the General Meeting. The General Meeting takes
decisions that fall within its competence under commercial law, such as decisions on amending the articles of association,
increasing and reducing share capital, electing, and removing members of the Council, approving the annual report, distributing
profit, and electing a statutory auditor. In addition, the General Meeting is responsible for approving significant changes to our
strategy, material changes to our key policies, and financial plans which anticipate an increase in capital, and engaging in other
significant activities. The General Meeting is entitled to decide on any other matter related to our activities at the request of
the Council or the Board. No General Meetings were convened in 2025, instead 14 decisions were made per capsulam.

Shareholders who hold at least 10% of the votes in Luminor Holding, our parent company, can appoint their pro rata proportion
of members to our Council. A sufficiently high number of independent members are elected to the Council to help ensure that
the interests of all internal and external stakeholders are considered, and that independent judgment is exercised where there
is an actual or potential conflict of interest. DNB, as the minority shareholder, has the right to request a review of our compliance
with the Compliance Risk Policy or ESG standards and other similar corporate social responsibility policies and standards, which
may be conducted by an external person or by the relevant requesting party.

CONDUCT
We aspire to the highest standards of ethical and professional conduct. Every employee is expected to know and follow our
values, ethical standards, and the principles of compliance and risk management. Each employee must abide by our code of
conduct and identify, prevent, and report bribery and corruption. We have developed corporate values – curiosity,
collaboration, and focus – and expected behaviours to reinforce the principles of compliance and risk management.

We promote an ethical culture and make every effort to identify, prevent, and manage conflicts of interest to ensure all
stakeholders are treated fairly and shareholder’s interests are protected. Principles for management of conflict of interest are
established by the Council which oversees its implementation and effectiveness. We hold mandatory training on conflict of
interest management to ensure that all employees have adequate knowledge of our policy and other relevant internal rules and
principles and that all activities within their responsibility are carried out in accordance with the rules. Any conflicts of interest
are considered when selecting new members to the Management Bodies and key function holders.

Following the gifts and events reporting procedure, our employees do not accept or offer gifts regardless of their value, nor
participate in events if doing so can be considered inappropriate, may be ethically questionable, or may affect the receiver or
giver in performing their duties. Our internal regulation provides specific examples to support employees in making decisions
on the appropriateness of gifts and events and handling such situations.

We manage information on a “need-to-know” basis, i.e., information is accessible only to employees who have a justified need
for such information to carry out their duties. To manage information flow, we have also established physical separation and
restricted access to information, or other specific arrangements, around and within certain business activities where
confidential customer information is handled.

DIVERSITY AND INCLUSION
We value and respect each employee for their differences. We are committed to building and maintaining a workforce
comprising individuals from diverse backgrounds, young people, persons with disabilities, and employees representing a variety
of cultures. Employees are supported and encouraged to develop their full potential and utilise their unique talents.

We recognize the importance of diverse composition of the Management Bodies. At 31 December 2025, female representation
on the Council was 33.3% as compared to a target of 40.0% The chairs of the Management Bodies review progress on gender
diversity goals as key performance indicators in their annual assessments. If targets are not met, the chairs document the
reasons, measures to be taken, and timeframe for measures to rectify the situation.

We do not tolerate any form of intimidation, bullying, scapegoating, or harassment in the workplace. We take measures to
protect employees from discrimination and have a process in place to discipline those who are in breach. We encourage
employees who feel they have been subject to discrimination to raise their concerns through the speak up process so that
corrective measures are applied.

DIVIDEND POLICY
We manage the Total Capital Ratio on a Luminor Group level at a Capital Target of the regulatory requirement (excluding P2G)
plus a Management Buffer of 150-300bps. We are committed to return excess capital to shareholders while maintaining a strong
capital position to support our business activities, stability and allow for profitable growth. Capital distribution will be made by
way of dividends or capital repatriations. Dividends are to be paid with a guideline of around 50% of the annual profit. All excess
capital above the Capital Target level is considered for distribution, meaning that the actual dividend pay-out ratio can be higher
or lower than 50%. A pay-out ratio higher than 50% will be considered if actual capital is above the Capital Target, and the
stress testing outcome supports a higher pay-out ratio. A pay-out ratio lower than 50% will be considered, e.g., if we assess
there are strong growth opportunities, if there are unforeseen changes in the regulatory framework for the capital calculations,
or if the macro environment or portfolio credit quality deteriorates significantly beyond what is reflected in the Management
Buffer. The actual pay-out ratio needs to be supported also by the outcome of the stress testing. Additional return of excess
capital resources will be considered in the form of extraordinary dividends/capital reductions when the CET1 capital can be
replaced by issuing Tier 2 and AT1 capital instruments.

KEY FUNCTION HOLDERS
The Key function holders are the Chief Financial Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, Chief Risk Officer, and Head of Internal
Audit, who each represent a function with significant influence over Luminor. The first three are members of the Board,
therefore the Head of Internal Audit is the only Key Function Holder in this sense.

SELECTION CRITERIA TO THE MANAGEMENT BODIES
Only people who have the necessary professional experience, necessary skills, and possess the appropriate character may be
members of our Management Bodies. In order to facilitate independent opinions as well as constructive challenging, we seek
for members that have an independence of mind and, in particular, are able to resist groupthink. The principles of selecting
members for Management Bodies, including assessing suitability and diversity, are set out in our internal regulations.
Appointments to Management Bodies are approved by the ECB.

We have established processes and regulations to address sudden or unexpected absences or departures of the chair or
members of the Board, and key function holders. By doing so we aim to ensure the transfer of knowledge, preservation of
organizational memory, and to support managerial and business continuity during periods of temporary or permanent
leadership changes.

The members of the Council are appointed amongst the nominees of Luminor Holding shareholders as provided in the
shareholders’ agreement, with each shareholder having the right to remove and replace a member appointed by it. The Council
and the Nomination and Governance Committee members, and the CEO, can identify the need to appoint a new Board member,
and the Nomination and Governance Committee provides guidance, selection criteria and service conditions for the respective
position and performs the suitability assessment.

The Council is our supervisory body which approves strategies, general principles of our activities, sets and monitors risk
tolerance and risk appetite, and supervises our activities, as well as those of the Board. General rules for convening meetings
and organisation of the work of the Council are set forth in our internal regulations, Commercial Code, Credit Institutions Act
and Articles of Association. Regular meetings of the Council ensure oversight over the Board along with additional meetings
when required. Decisions are passed by simple majority participating in the meeting. Decisions submitted to the Council shall
be discussed before by respective committee of the Council. The Council is required to meet at least quarterly. In 2025, the
Council held 16 meetings and adopted 26 decisions in circulation. The members elect from among themselves a chair, who is
responsible for the effective functioning of the Council, coordinates its work and contributes to the flow of information within
the Council and the Board.

The Board is our executive body which directs day-to-day activities pursuant to the strategies and general principles of activities
approved by the Council. The Board reviews proposals and explanations presented to it, takes decisions, and reports
appropriately to the Council. General rules for organisation of the work of the Board, including rules for the convening meetings,
voting procedures, and decision-making process, responsibilities and number of Board members, are set forth in our internal
regulations, Commercial Code, Credit Institutions Act and Articles of Association. Decisions are passed by a simple majority of
members participating at the meeting. In case of equality of the votes, the Chair or, in their absence, the Deputy chair of the
Board, has a casting vote. Members of the Board are elected and removed by the Council. The Council appoints a Chair from
the members of the Board. The Chair, or any two Board members, legally represent the Bank. Areas of responsibility are divided
between the members to suit their skills, expertise, and responsibilities.

INTERNAL CONTROL FRAMEWORK IN CONNECTION WITH THE PREPARATION OF THE ANNUAL REPORT
We aim to ensure that our financial reporting is in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, applicable laws,
and regulations, and our financial statements provide a true and fair view of the financial position. The Board has responsibility
to set, approve and monitor processes and controls intended to ensure the integrity of the accounting, financial and non-
financial reporting systems, and preparation of these financial statements pursuant to the relevant law.

The Board has delegated to the Finance Division the responsibility for financial reporting and establishment of the arrangements
and internal control aimed at ensuring the integrity of the accounting and financial reporting systems, including financial and
operational controls and compliance with the law and relevant standards. Financial reporting is subject to an internal control
framework that entails adequate, clear, transparent, and effective routines for reporting, monitoring, and follow-up processes.

Our internal control framework aims to ensure: effective and efficient operations; prudent conduct of business; sound change
management; adequate identification, measurement, and treatment of risk; compliance with laws, regulations, supervisory
requirements and our internal policies and procedures, processes, rules and decisions; sound administrative and accounting
procedures; and, reliability of financial and non-financial information internally and externally.

We have a ‘three-lines’ internal control framework. The first line, which consists of our business divisions, and support divisions
and departments, own their risks and are responsible for ongoing managing of risks according to our policies, procedures, and
controls. To mitigate process and reporting risk we have segregated duties, and applied IT general controls, entity and process-
level controls, and preventive and detective controls.

The second line is an independent control function authorised and responsible to monitor and control that the first line adheres
to our risk appetite and risk management framework and all applicable rules and regulations. The second line, which consists
of Compliance and Risk divisions, are responsible for internal second line control over financial reporting in their respective
areas. Our internal controls ensure that financial reporting is true and fair and that external financial statements are prepared
in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, applicable laws and regulations.

The third line consists of Internal Audit division, which is an independent internal audit function. It conducts risk based and
general audits and reviews that the internal governance arrangements, processes, and mechanisms are sound and effective,
implemented and consistently applied. The Internal Audit division evaluates independently whether operations and related
controls, risk management and governance processes and structures are functioning, adequate and effective to enhance our
ability to reach our business objectives. All activities, including financial reporting process fall within the scope of Internal Audit,
which provides independent, objective assurance that financial reporting is adequate and in compliance with applicable internal
and external regulatory requirements. Internal Audit provides the Council, the Audit Committee and the Board with a written
report regarding their activities and evaluation on governance, risk management and internal control processes.

The Council’s Audit Committee oversees our accounting and financial reporting. It oversees the establishment of accounting
policies, including tax accounting, as well as the budgeting process, reviews and monitors the financial reporting process,
reviews our consolidated financial reports and considers whether they are complete, consistent with information known to the
Audit Committee’s members, and reflect appropriate accounting policies and principles, as well as provides the Council with
recommendations aimed at ensuring reliability and objectivity of consolidated financial reports, integrity of the financial
reporting process and make recommendations to the Council for the approval of consolidated financial reports.

Furthermore, the Audit Committee is responsible for monitoring the effectiveness of the statutory audit of these financial
statements, and assurance of the sustainability statement, to ensure the statements are prepared according to applicable laws,
regulations, and standards, including reviewing and monitoring the independence and objectivity of the statutory auditors.

MANAGEMENT OF BRANCHES
We operate in Latvia and Lithuania via branches. The branches enter into agreements and undertake obligations on our behalf,
acquire other rights and assume other duties, consistent with the law and their mandate. Branch managers are appointed by
the Council and are accountable for the activities of their branch.

=== pdf p.37 ===
MANAGEMENT OF SUBSIDIARIES
All subsidiaries are separate legal entities which follow our values, code of conduct, and policies. Individuals with relevant
knowledge, skills and experience, and with consideration of collective suitability, are appointed to the supervisory councils and
members of the management boards are full time employees of the Bank or subsidiary. Subsidiaries’ chief executive officers
and management boards are responsible for the implementation of the decisions taken by the Management Bodies. The
supervisory councils (or management boards) follow legal and regulatory provisions when reporting to the Board.

Certain subsidiaries are supervised by the relevant Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian financial supervision authorities. Governing
bodies of the subsidiaries ensure that the subsidiary operated according to legal or regulatory requirements. The
proportionality principle shall always be considered when applying regulatory requirements, which includes, but is not limited
to the size of the subsidiary as well as the size of its customer base, nature and complexity of business and products, and gravity
of risk. Dividend payments are governed by internal regulations.

AUDITORS
We have been audited by AS PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) since 2018. Lauri Past is the lead partner for the audit.

GOVERNANCE OVERVIEW OF ESG
The individual and collective suitability of each Board member is observed continuously to make certain they remain fit and
proper for their task. The Nomination and Governance Committee of the Council is responsible for the suitability assessment,
assessment and re-assessment of individual and collective suitability of the Board, assessment and re-assessment of individual
and collective suitability of the Council. While assessing their suitability, adequacy of knowledge, skills and experience is
assessed. Among others, a knowledge of environmental, social, and corporate governance topics is assessed. Council members
demonstrate knowledge in the ESG, including an understanding of sustainability standards and how to contribute to our
sustainable development, and collectively their knowledge and expertise are assessed as sufficient.

To keep their knowledge up to date, both Management Bodies have training plans aligned with regulatory guidelines. The training
plans are approved each year and include ESG related trainings. In 2025, members of the Management Bodies received training
on the taxonomy reporting and climate-related risks. Additionally, tailored training sessions and individual consultations are
offered to Board members to address specific needs. To fulfil their obligations members can access experts for advice or
training and may request information internally.

Newly appointed members of our Management Bodies receive individual induction plans to help them integrate into the
organisation and their appointed role. Members are expected to complete their individual plans and be proactive in seeking
further opportunities to raise their knowledge including becoming familiar with our strategy, culture, and risk management, and
understanding of sustainability standards.

The Council approves the organisational structure, the mandates of the members of the Board, the Sustainability Policy, the
Risk Policy, and the Risk Appetite Framework-Policy, which integrates responsibility for ESG risk drivers, and oversees the
implementation of ESG risk management including strategies and due diligence processes.

Oversight of sustainability‑related impacts, risks and opportunities is exercised by the Council, as defined in our Sustainability
Policy. The Council is the highest governance body with formal responsibility for sustainability matters. Its responsibilities
include: Setting our sustainability objectives and ensuring their alignment with our strategy; overseeing sustainability‑related
risks and opportunities, including monitoring the effectiveness of the associated internal control and risk management
framework; reviewing the Board’s execution of sustainability‑related activities and performance; assessing results of the DMA
which follows Board approval; evaluating regular ESG reports and monitoring key sustainability indicators; reviewing and
recommending the Sustainability Statement within the Annual Report for approval by the shareholders.

The Council monitors the risks we face, including ESG risks, potential impacts, and emerging scenarios, via regular reporting
and ad hoc risk and sustainability assessments. The Council is responsible for steering the execution of the strategy, which
considers material impacts, risks and opportunities and risk appetite, and through its committees receives an over-arching view
of the risk landscape and the progress of the strategy. IROs are integrated with business units, which aligns risk management
with operational activities and decision-making processes.

In accordance with Sustainability Policy, the Board is responsible for: developing the Sustainability Policy and the sustainability
objectives within our strategy and ensuring that strategic sustainability objectives, defined by the Council, are performed;
ensuring proper identification of material sustainability-related impacts, risks and opportunities through a comprehensive DMA;
approving the results of the DMA and proposing it for review of the Council; approving Transition plan for the management of
ESG-related material risks; ensuring adequate assessment of the sustainability-related risks and their integration into risk limit
setting; monitoring and directing the management of material sustainability-related impacts, risks and opportunities through
comprehensive integration into the group strategy and business practices, including the financial plan; ensuring application of
ESG-linked remuneration principles and monitoring their alignment with ESG-related risk appetite and with transition plans and
ensuring transparent sustainability reporting and public disclosures.

Council approves the mandate of each Board member. According to mandates, each member of the Board has a distinct area
of expertise and members, other than the CEO, act as head of a division. As such they are accountable for the risks within their
bailiwick, which collectively creates a comprehensive oversight structure.
