The Chief Financial Officer is responsible for setting, maintaining, and updating our ESG framework, for preparing quantitative
and/or qualitative sustainability disclosures and annual corporate sustainability reports as required by EU and national
legislation, for monitoring climate and environmental risk drivers' impact on our business model, operations and its value chain
and monitoring our impact on ESG factors.

The Chief Risk Officer ensures the implementation of overall risk strategy, and lead the defining of risk appetite, is responsible
for continuous identifying and monitoring of material risks, aggregate and emerging risk, monitors the actual risk profile of the
Bank, and facilitates the implementation of the risk management framework, including Risk Policy, Risk Appetite Framework and
other risk related internal regulations, risk limits and risk controls. CRO is also responsible for reporting risks to the Board and
the Council, either through the Risk Committee or directly. in addition, the CRO has the authority to raise concerns and escalate
issues directly to the Council, particularly regarding developments that significantly affect or may affect our risk profile.

The CFO collaborates with the CRO to develop an appropriate risk appetite aligned with our strategy and risk-taking capacity.

CFO monitors climate and environmental risk drivers' impact on our business model, operations and its value chain, and ensures
associated information’s submission, where relevant, to the Management Bodies. CFO also monitors our impact on ESG factors,
and ensure associated information’s submission, where relevant, to the Management Bodies.

We regularly monitor key risk indicators and maintain reporting systems to track risk exposure and incidents and performs
reporting by means of the quarterly risk report.

CRO is responsible for reporting all risks to the Board and Council through the Council Risk committee. CRO reports on all
material inherent and residual risks, provide relevant independent information, analysis and expert judgment on risk exposures
to the Board and Council and provides aggregated quarterly risk reports to the Board and Council.

Risk committee through quarterly risk reports monitors the implementation of ESG risk drivers in Risk Management Framework.
Council monitors regular reports and relevant data on our risk position, including causes for changes and loss events.

We have established a procedure regulating roles and process of executing the annual DMA. All Risk Division Departments act
as ESG-related risk controllers and review and challenge ESG-related risks linked with the risks controlled by the Risk Division.
They participate in the DMA related discussions, where relevant; and provide review and challenge of the ESG-related risk
assessments including review of evidence and documentation of feedback. Risk division also ensures that DMA outcomes
associated with ESG-related risks are considered for the purpose of the Risk Identification and Risk Materiality Assessments

Board provides their input to IRO identification through a questionnaire or focus group discussion or validation of the final list
of material IROs, as well as approves the DMA outcome (the final list of Material IROs) and submit this for information purposes
to the Council.

Our strategy for sustainability is embedded within the strategy and approved by the Council. It defines our long-term
sustainability ambition and outlines key objectives and targets, which address the material IROs for our business. All
sustainability objectives and targets are operationalized through internal governance, and business planning processes, relying
on the management of material IROs and transition planning.

Group Sustainability Department, part of Finance Division, reviews the Sustainability strategy annually and suggests updates to
promote ESG principles, develops and proposes ESG targets for various divisions, and is responsible for sustainability monitoring
and reporting, including this annual sustainability statement. Together with the Risk and the People and culture divisions, the
Department trains staff to foster a risk-aware culture, while continuous feedback mechanisms across all functions keep risk
controls effective and aligned with evolving regulatory requirements and business needs.

INTEGRATION OF SUSTAINABILITY RELATED PERFORMANCE IN THE INCENTIVE SCHEME
Our Remuneration Policy integrates ESG targets into Employees' annual performance criteria through Performance fee
components with Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) that track whether targets have been met. Sustainability considerations are
integrated into performance with ESG‑related targets (incl. C&E risks) applied at appropriate organizational levels rather than
always directly cascaded. Social sustainability is embedded through the Risk Culture framework, while environmental aspects
are reflected through capability building and decarbonization and emissions‑related targets assigned to relevant managerial
levels.

The policy is applied through the Performance Fee for Staff procedure. Performance Fee is not a guaranteed payment and
depends on whether performance criteria or KPIs are met, as well as taking into account impact of performance fee pay-out
to capital and liquidity or overall economic situation .At the beginning of measurement period, the Council approves the
performance criteria for the Members of the Board, Branch Managers, Key Function Holders, and Heads of Internal Control
Functions, and sets the overall performance criteria like objectives and KPIs. Those performance criteria are then cascaded to
Level 2 (L2) managers and onwards. ESG considerations are integrated into Luminor’s performance management system
through dedicated sustainability targets that form 5–10% of the annual objectives for Group and Division Heads, with divisions
cascading these expectations to their departments and units, who define the most relevant ESG KPIs for their activities. In line
with internal policy, unit head of each employee must define and incorporate into performance discussions ESG‑related targets
when cascaded to the unit. While the Performance Management IT system does not apply predefined thresholds or
formula‑based scoring for ESG, performance is evaluated holistically, and sustainability performance can influence the
Performance rating. The system also includes automatic performance adjustments in cases of conduct breaches or incomplete
mandatory training, ensuring accountability and alignment with Luminor’s values.

There are no predefined thresholds and no formula‑based scoring—performance is evaluated holistically. Sustainability
performance can positively impact the Performance Fee when targets are achieved. It cannot negatively reduce the award.
Reductions apply only in cases of conduct breaches or incomplete mandatory training.

SUMMARY OF REPORTING LINES, MANAGEMENT AND OVERSIGHT OVER SUSTAINABILITY MATTERS
We have defined our governance model, roles and accountabilities for ESG risks and are integrating them into our existing
policies. Our governance structure helps us take strategic decisions to manage the risks we face including climate-related and
environmental risks, to set goals, and to monitor progress towards these goals

Our management bodies are updated about material impacts, risks, and opportunities at least once a quarter. The Sustainability
department reports on sustainability-related strategic initiatives and relevant KPIs covering the climate change related impacts,
risks and opportunities, Risk division reports on risk and resilience analysis, while People & Culture department reports on the
gender gap in the annual remuneration report. For each material risk, a transition plan is approved by the Board, and the
progress against the plan is reported by the transition plan or material matter owner and by Risk Division each quarter.

Our first line, second- and third- line monitor compliance of our actions with our policies and procedures. When internal control
functions review processes that include due‑diligence activities, they will also verify that the due‑diligence steps were

completed correctly. Their findings will be reported to the relevant management bodies. Second line reports the results of the
activities to the Board and, the third line informs the Board and reports to the Council on its work and recommendation.

When the management bodies oversee strategy, decisions on major transactions, and the risk management process, they
consider the impacts, risks, and opportunities presented in these reports. These reports let the Council see the impact of
strategy execution. All material IROs connected to material matters, as listed in the section 'Change to the process from the
previous reporting period' are reviewed and discussed in Risk Committee and in Supervisory Council annually as part of the
double materiality assessment (DMA).

We have incorporated ESG-related risks as a component of our Remuneration policy. These ESG-related risks are integrated
into the variable remuneration components, with KPIs that track whether targets for performance are met. At the start of the
measurement period, the Council approves the overall performance criteria for the year, for members of the Board selected
employees. These performance criteria are then cascaded, with each level incorporating sustainability risks and our voluntary
sustainability commitments into their performance criteria. These commitments encompass all areas of ESG, including climate
and environmental concerns. Financial performance is monitored on a weekly basis by the Board, while KPIs are reviewed
quarterly, while a report on performance is reported each quarter submitted to the Council.

Management bodies approve our material IROs, the related material matters for disclosure in the annual sustainability statement
and thresholds for financial and impact materiality. The DMA is coordinated by the Sustainability Department and foreseen to
be conducted every three years. In the interim years, in case there is no significant methodology update, we use the earlier
assessment outcomes. Maintaining the earlier assessment is acceptable if there have been no material changes in our structure,
or in external factors that could affect new or existing IROs. Significant alterations like major mergers or acquisitions, entry into
new sectors, or operational overhauls, are scrutinised for any possible implication for human rights or public reputation. The
periodic review lets our sustainability disclosures to respond to evolving circumstances.

We have a dedicated Double Materiality Assessment Procedure and Sustainability Reporting Standard to create transparency
in addressing ESG topics. This framework has four elements for annual disclosures and for our strategy. First, the DMA evaluates
various aspects of ESG within our operations. Second, the C&E RBE process identifies critical areas within climate and
environment risk factors space, delineates specific impacts, and formulates strategic responses tailored to our operations. It is
also an input for prioritising Climate Risk Stress Testing within the credit portfolio by focusing on the economic activities or risk
drivers affected.

Third, the ESG Risk Drivers Impact Assessment is run during the Risk Policy review as part of the broader Risk Materiality
Assessment (RMA) process to quantify the impact of ESG risk drivers on various risk types and sub-types within our Risk
Taxonomy which gives us a comprehensive understanding of how ESG considerations intersect with existing risk categories.
Fourth, and finally, the Climate Risk Stress Testing assesses the risk exposures from climate and environmental factors. By stress
testing our operations we can assess vulnerabilities, prioritise material risk drivers, and inform the strategic decision-making
and risk limit-setting processes effectively.

DUE DILIGENCE PROCESSES
We perform ESG due diligence on our suppliers, customers, and investment activities. These processes are governed by our
Sustainability Policy and ESG Due Diligence Standard, in accordance with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human
Rights and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. ESG due diligence topics comprise environmental issues,
including climate change and biodiversity, social issues, including human and labour rights, and governance practices, including
ethical business conduct.

We conduct risk-based due diligence, considering the severity, nature and likelihood of the actual and potential impacts of our
business on the environment and society. We focus our effort where the consequences and probability of negative impacts are
the highest. Compliance with the Exclusion List, that is part of our Sustainability Policy and contains ESG related restrictions, is
ensured within our credit, sourcing and investment processes.

Customer due diligence is conducted at the start of a customer relationship, and on an ongoing basis. The nature of the
questions we ask depends on the risk level of the customer and the size of their credit exposure. We focus our due diligence

Due diligence is performed for all new suppliers before the start of a relationship and is then reviewed periodically, with a
frequency that depends on the Tier of the supplier. For suppliers we have developed due diligence questionnaires by levels of
criticality and importance of a supplier to us. The questionnaires for Tier 1 and 2 suppliers have specific questions on ESG
related business practices. Where gaps are identified they serve as input in risk assessments. During 2025 we engaged our Tier
1 and 2 suppliers to address ESG due diligence gaps identified in 2024. We require that all suppliers from outside the EU and
EEA confirm they adhere to our Code of Responsible Business Conduct for Third Parties (part of our Code of Conduct) or
provide their internal code with similar rules to that of our Code of Conduct in all material aspects.

Our Discretionary Portfolio Management (DPM) business and Pension fund management subsidiaries, integrate ESG due
diligence into their investment processes. We assess ESG risks for all financial instruments before including them into our
investment offering and reassessed their characteristics each year. We require third party fund managers to be signatories to
the United Nations Principles of Responsible Investment (PRI), where feasible and relevant. If available and relevant, we may
consider external ESG risk ratings for financial instruments in our risk assessment.

IRO IN THE STRATEGY PROCESS
Our management bodies are accountable for our strategy, which is governed by the Business Model Risk Policy and Strategy
Planning Procedure. Our strategy and associated Financial plan are reviewed annually integrating material IRO treatment
approaches. The strategy implementation is monitored by our management bodies including the use of Key Performance
Indicators (KPIs).

Our strategy process links with other processes like the internal capital adequacy assessment process (ICAAP) and the internal
liquidity adequacy assessment process (ILAAP), which incorporate the outcome of the double materiality assessment (DMA) and
climate and environmental risk materiality assessment (C&E RMA) processes. Risks identified are considered throughout the
entire process, including the initial strategy discussions, financial planning, Risk Appetite Statement (RAS) and limits reviews, and
stress testing.

The material impacts resulting from the DMA in 2025 are described in the related material topic sections of the report, with a
description of how the material negative and positive impacts affect, or are likely to affect, people or the environment, and




                                                                                               Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025            43

=== pdf p.44 ===
whether and how the material impacts originate from or are connected to our strategy and business model by having an actual
or potential financially negative or positive impact on us. These sections also provide the expected time horizons for the material
impacts and a description of the nature of the activities or business relationships and affected stakeholders through which we
may experience the material impacts.

In 2025, an assessment of current and short‑term financial effects of material sustainability‑related risks and opportunities was
performed as part of the DMA, RMA and stress‑testing exercises. The assessment concluded that these risks and opportunities
do not currently have a material impact on the financial position, financial performance or cash flows. Furthermore, none of
the identified material risks or opportunities present a significant risk of material adjustment to the carrying amounts of assets
or liabilities within the next 12 months. Our strategy and business model are designed to remain resilient in the face of material
sustainability-related impacts, risks, and opportunities. For every material risk, we develop transition plans that are
scenario‑based, aligned with our strategic objectives and consistent with regulatory expectations. These plans incorporate the
results of our short‑, medium‑ and long‑term climate risk assessments and support ongoing portfolio steering and risk mitigation.

Changes in material IROs
This year we improved our DMA methodology to reflect more closely with ESRS requirements. As a result, the IRO analysis
related to these three topics: Circular economy, Own workforce, and governance-related issues including Business conduct
and Cybersecurity, did not meet our updated thresholds for disclosure-relevant materiality such as Circular economy, Own
workforce, and governance-related issues including Business conduct and Cybersecurity. The thresholds we adopted
previously led to an overestimation of disclosure relevance for certain topics. The updated thresholds, including a secondary
financial materiality threshold, ensure that only the topics with significant actual or potential impacts and financial relevance
are disclosed, enhancing the clarity and utility of our reporting. We report on material topics — climate change, biodiversity and
ecosystems, and consumers and end-users — aligned with ESRS. For topics that were material in 2024 but are no longer material
this year, we disclose progress against previously reported targets and plans. No additional entity-specific disclosures are
included beyond the ESRS requirements.

Stakeholder engagement
We maintain a structured approach to understanding the interests and views of our key stakeholders as they relate to our
strategy and business model. Through our annual DMA we engage with a wide range of stakeholders using focus groups, surveys,
and analysis of public reports. The insights gathered are assessed systematically and translated into IROs, which inform strategic
planning and sustainability priorities. This ensures our business model remains responsive to stakeholder expectations and
aligned with evolving sustainability-related risks and opportunities.

Our stakeholder engagement reveals customer preferences with regards to sector or activity specific financial flows, identify
potential need to adjust our financing strategy and or our exclusion list, and reveals where we may enhance our approach. To
understand the perspectives of customers and how this impacts our portfolio, we also analyse the impact of C&E risks on our
Business Environment (C&E RBE), and run C&E Risk Impact Materiality on our main risk types

The C&E RBE analysis and the Risk Taxonomy Review and Risk Materiality Assessment, which are inputs to our DMA, inform
climate change risk drivers which may be material for us and which portfolios they effect. Once a risk is identified as material,
it is stress-tested via ICAAP and ILAAP process to evaluate whether the taxonomy needs to be updated, and risk mitigation
approach and measures defined such as developing new products or setting risk limits.

As part of the DMA, we present an overview to the Board and the Council, outlining how stakeholder engagement was
conducted. The key stakeholder views are translated into IROs during the DMA process and assessed accordingly. Only
disclosure-relevant material IROs are submitted to the Board for approval and to Council for oversight. Additionally, the
outcomes of other large-scale stakeholder engagements—such as our biannual employee pulse survey—are presented to the
Board to ensure continued alignment with stakeholder expectations.

ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION
Disclosures pursuant to Article 8 of EU Taxonomy Regulation
As a central pillar of the EU’s sustainable finance framework, the EU Taxonomy Regulation establishes a unified system for
identifying environmentally sustainable (EU Taxonomy aligned) economic activities and sets disclosure requirements designed
to enhance transparency.

Integrating the EU Taxonomy into our business operations primarily involves complying with its reporting obligations, which in
turn requires a detailed assessment of our activities and investments. This assessment enables us to evaluate the extent to
which our financing and investment activities contribute to the EU’s environmental objectives—covering climate change
mitigation and adaptation, water and marine resources, the circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and biodiversity
protection. It also helps us better understand prevailing market conditions and emerging sustainability trends.

Although Paris alignment remains one of our key priorities, we have not yet established specific Key Performance Indicators
(KPIs) linked to the EU Taxonomy’s Green Asset Ratio (GAR). This is primarily due to the ongoing evolution of the regulatory
landscape surrounding the EU Taxonomy. Until there is greater clarity regarding the final scope, framework, detailed
interpretations, and data availability associated with the EU Taxonomy requirements, setting robust long-term KPIs tied to the
GAR or similar metrics is challenging. Still, we are continuously strengthening our understanding of the EU Taxonomy and its
implications.

The EU Taxonomy reporting is also heavily affected by the data availability. Therefore, our EU Taxonomy report is subject to
continuous change due to increased quality of data collected from customers and enhanced market practices for the CSRD
related disclosures.

RESTATEMENTS
In line with EU Commission’s guidance, restatements may be necessary when there are significant changes or updates to the
methodology or data used in the initial reporting period. Due to enhancement in data availability, we have reassessed the
counterparties classified as CSRD companies. Due these adjustments, the overall GAR for 2024 remain unchanged at 3.6%
(based on turnover KPI of the counterparties) and increased to 3.7% (based on CapEx KPI of the counterparties).

Our EU Taxonomy report follows the templates established in the Disclosure Delegated Act as amended by the Commission
Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/73 of 4 July 2025. Therefore, to ensure consistency and comparability, we have restated the
main EU Taxonomy KPIs presented in Template 0 using the revised methodology introduced by the amended Disclosure
Delegated Act. Under the revised methodological framework, the value of assets covered by GAR denominator has reduced,
leading to an increase in GAR ratio. As a result, Luminor’s 2024 GAR increased to 5.9% (based on turnover KPI of the
counterparties) compared to previously reported 3.6%, and 6.1% (based on CapEx KPI of the counterparties) compared to 3.7%.

Furthermore, exposures to local governments and assets under management have been reassessed as not material for the 2024
reporting year, in accordance with Article 4, paragraphs 1(a) and 1(f) of the amended Disclosure Delegated Act, respectively. This
ensures that the same assessment approach is applied consistently across both reporting years.

BASIS OF REPORTING
Our EU Taxonomy report is prepared on the basis of the scope of the prudential consolidation determined in accordance with
the EU Regulation No 575/2013 following the reporting templates applicable for credit institutions.

Within the reporting templates, we cover consolidated information on the Bank and its subsidiaries: (i) activities of the Leasing
Subsidiaries are consolidated and reported as lending activities to financial undertakings, non-financial undertakings and retail
customers; (ii) activities of Asset Management Subsidiaries are consolidated and reported as assets under management; (iii)
concerning Maksekeskus AS, that operates in e-commerce payment industry, Bank’s EU Taxonomy report shall represent its
activities within KPIs on fees and commissions for services other than lending starting with 2028.




46     Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025

=== pdf p.47 ===
In our EU Taxonomy report, the on-balance sheet items are reported in gross carrying amount. Gross carrying amount is the
amortised cost of a financial asset before adjusting for any loss allowance. Because of this, the total assets in the EU Taxonomy
templates are 109 million EUR higher than the total assets reported in the balance sheet in Luminor Bank Annual Report. The
difference is comprised of loss allowances across several assets.

Determination of EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment
Following requirements stemming from Disclosure Delegated Act, we disclose information on EU Taxonomy eligibility and
alignment of the exposures (loans, advances, debt securities) to financial and non-financial CSRD companies (i.e. such
companies that are subject to the EU Taxonomy Regulation reporting requirements themselves), local governments, households
(mortgage lending, renovation loans and vehicle leasing) and collaterals obtained by taking possession. Methodology for
determining EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment of the above indicated categories, as well as data limitations, are described
below.

Exposure to CSRD companies
The CSRD companies were identified based on publicly available and internal data. Our reporting covers large public interest
companies and parent public interest companies of a large group (including their subsidiaries) that have published their EU
Taxonomy reports.

For the calculation of the amount of EU Taxonomy eligible and aligned exposures to CSRD companies, we evaluated use of
proceeds of exposures and considered the gross carrying amount of general-purpose loans, debt securities and equities of
relevant accounting portfolios weighted by the respective counterparties’ KPIs.

Main data constrains and limitations related to CSRD companies are absence of central external database for the list of CSRD
companies which may result in omission in our reporting. Furthermore, due to unavailability of the counterparties’ respective
KPIs for year-end 2025, the assessment and disclosure of EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment for the relevant exposures was
based on the counterparties’ 2024 EU Taxonomy reports data.

Retail exposures
Disclosure Delegated Act distinguishes reporting of retail exposures among residential real estate exposures, loans granted for
house renovation purpose and vehicle leasing. The exposures to residential real estate are considered as financing EU Taxonomy
eligible economic activities in case a household loan is collateralised by residential immovable property.

We have reported as EU Taxonomy aligned those mortgage loans that comply, based on our assessment and internally available
data, with the substantial contribution criteria applicable for acquisition and ownership of buildings in respect of climate change
mitigation objective and do no significant harm (DNSH) criteria to climate change adaptation objective established by the
Climate Delegated Act. Minimum safeguards have not been evaluated for residential real estate exposures based on the
requirements established in the Disclosure Delegated Act as well as interpretation provided in the Final Report on Minimum
Safeguards by Platform on Sustainable Finance, dated October 2022. Further, we have not evaluated whether the mortgaged
real estate fall under the category of buildings with a total floor area of 5,000 square meters or more, nor have we assessed the
requirements related to this specific classification because of data limitations.

In Lithuania and Latvia, loans collateralised by buildings constructed before 31 December 2020 with an EPC class A or higher,
as well as buildings classified within the top 15% of the national building stock based on PED (as defined in publicly available
studies by the national banking associations), were identified as EU Taxonomy aligned. In Estonia, due to a lack of PED data in
our systems, we could not apply the top-15% criterion, and only exposures collateralised by EPC class A buildings were
recognised as aligned.

For buildings built after 31 December 2020, compliance with the substantial contribution criteria for climate change mitigation
objective was assessed in relation to buildings’ PED being at least 10% lower than national thresholds of nearly zero-energy
buildings (NZEB). EU Taxonomy aligned exposures conforming with this criterion were identified for Lithuanian and Latvian
mortgage portfolios. The alignment of Estonian mortgages could not be confirmed due to lack of PED data on individual building
level in our systems.

For the purposes to verify compliance with DNSH to climate change adaptation objective, we have utilised the results of analysis
of C&E risks on business environment for retail mortgage portfolio (further information about the process can be found in

With reference to the household renovation loans, we have adopted the conservative approach and only loans with the purpose
of renovation, indicated in our lending products supporting systems, were considered as EU Taxonomy eligible exposures. In
case of any uncertainty in respect of lending purpose (that is data limitation for the purpose of EU Taxonomy reporting), loans
were not reported as EU Taxonomy eligible. The EU Taxonomy alignment of renovation loans of retail customers could not be
established due to absence of data required for screening substantial contribution criteria as well as DNSH criteria.

As for the vehicle leasing, for the EU Taxonomy eligibility reporting purposes only those exposures that are generated after 1
January 2022 (the date of application of the disclosure requirements) are reported. Due to unavailable data for screening of
the DNSH criteria, the EU Taxonomy alignment of motor vehicle loans of retail customers was not determined.

Exposures to local governments
Our classification of local government entities is based on the European System of Accounts (ESA) definition, in line with
established financial reporting standards. These exposures were assessed as not material for 2024 and 2025 in accordance with
Article 4, paragraph 1a, of the Disclosure Delegated Act as exposures to local governments amount to 2.8% and 3.8%,
respectively, of the total on-balance-sheet exposures with known use of proceeds covered by GAR denominator. Therefore,
the assessment of EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment of these exposures was not performed.

Assets under management
Under asset under management exposures, we consolidate exposures pertaining to discretionary portfolio management service
provided by the Bank as well as pension funds management activities performed by Asset Management Subsidiaries.

As revenues generated from assets under management activities accounted for 1.82% and 2.1% of total net revenue for 2024
and 2025, respectively, KPI for asset under management is not reported in accordance with Article 4, paragraph 1f of the
Disclosure Delegated Act, and EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment evaluation of the respective exposures was not performed.

counterparties) compared to year-end 2024 KPIs of 415.2 million EUR. The absence of growth in the GAR is therefore not driven
by a reduction in EU Taxonomy aligned assets, but rather by a significantly larger increase (approximately 780 million EUR) in
total GAR-covered assets. As a result, the growth rate of total covered assets outpaced the growth of aligned exposures, leading
to a proportional reduction in the GAR KPI despite the positive development in the aligned asset volume.

The growth in Luminor EU Taxonomy aligned exposures is mainly stemming from the increase of the portfolio of EU Taxonomy
aligned mortgage loans, which grew by 28.8 million EUR through new lending and data availability improvements, and to the
rising exposure to CSRD companies and their subsidiaries. The full set of EU Taxonomy reporting templates applicable for credit
institutions are included in the Note 1 within the Notes to the Sustainability Statement.

Climate change
We are committed to becoming carbon neutral by 2050. To achieve this, we have embedded climate and environmental
objectives into our strategy and have developed a Climate and Environment Transition Plan. Furthermore, we have prioritised
SDG 13, including to mitigate, adapt to, and reduce the impact of climate change. The policies, targets and actions disclosed are
part of our C&E Transition plan and were developed based on the IROs identified through the Double Materiality Assessment
(DMA) process we conducted and informed by our Analysis of the Impact of Climate & Environmental Risks on the Business
Environment (C&E RBE).

POLICIES
Our approach to climate change mitigation and adaptation is guided by our Sustainability Policy, which sets overarching
objectives and principles for managing climate-related impacts, risks and opportunities. These are implemented through the
Sustainability Standard developed in 2025 and supported by internal regulations and procedures that ensure integration across
all business functions and subsidiaries. In addition to climate neutrality in our own operations by 2050 and reducing financed
emissions in line with the Paris Agreement, we are committed to support customer transition through integration of C&E factors
in credit and investment decisions. Accordingly, we require credible transition plans for high-risk sectors, restrict financing for
coal, oil shale, and peat-based energy production unless a transition plan is in place, and minimise environmental impacts,
protect biodiversity, and promote resource efficiency. Furthermore, we are committed to comply with ESG regulations and
maintain transparent reporting, embed material ESG risks into risk management and manage them via transition planning, and
expand sustainability-related products to support a low-carbon and climate-resilient economy.

Integration into our governance and operations is achieved through DMA, Process of Analysis of the impact of climate and
environmental risks on our business environment (C&E RBE), Sustainability Reporting Standard, ESG Due Diligence Standard,
and Risk Materiality Assessment (RMA) process. In 2025, we developed a Sustainability-Related Lending Standard and updated
the Product Management Procedure to update the framework to define and classify all sustainability-related lending products
and so set the foundation for future development of sustainability related loan products.

Our section on 'Policies, Procedures and Standards' gives further details on the regulations we use to identify, assess and
mitigate our climate and environmental impacts including their scope and approval bodies. Together, these frameworks ensure
sustainability objectives integration in the internal governance and their consistency across the organisation. And our value
chain.

Our Sustainability Policy and supporting regulations are developed with consideration of the interests of key stakeholders,
including customers, employees, and regulators. Policy proposals follow internal governance and external applicable regulatory




50      Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025

=== pdf p.51 ===
frameworks such as the ones established by EBA, ECB and EU Green Deal, and are aligned with our customer segments to
integrate customer perspectives, ensure sales feasibility, and confirm compliance with applicable regulations.

TARGETS
We have set targets for mitigating climate change by reducing GHG emissions. We are committed to become carbon neutral by
2050, to become able to decarbonise our portfolio, and to reduce our Scope 1, 2, and 3 operating emissions) by 42% in absolute
emissions by 2030, compared to 2024 baseline. Currently, we have not set any targets related to climate change adaptation.

In 2025, we reviewed our Science Based Targets initiative to ensure continued alignment with emerging guidance. We have not
resubmitted updated targets to SBTi, and the decision regarding resubmission remains under consideration. The targets for
reducing our emissions from operations are derived from emission reduction pathways that could limit global warming to 1.5°C.
The target of reducing emissions to net zero covers all three scopes of GHG emissions without residual emissions and is based
on conclusive scientific environmental evidence. Achieving the target will mean that our impacts on climate change are in line,
for example, with the European Climate Law, particularly the goal of climate neutrality by 2050 and with a climate scenario of a
temperature rise of 1.5°C as defined by the IPCC.

Levers for reducing emissions
In 2025, we developed a plan to reduce our own Scope 3 emissions for material Scope 3 emission categories as classified in
section 'Methodologies'. In this report, the term “our own Scope 3 emissions” refers specifically to Scope 3 categories 1–14,
which arise from upstream and downstream value‑chain activities linked to our operations. We use this term solely, to distinguish
these categories from our Scope 3 category 15 financed emissions, which represent the dominant share of our overall Scope 3
footprint and relate to the climate impact of our financing activities rather than our operational value chain. We further aim to
neutralise residual GHG emissions from our own operations through carbon removal using voluntary contributions. We have
financed professional restoration works in Lithuania and organised an employee wetland restoration activity in one of the Baltic
countries, alternating location by year.

We have set short-term decarbonisation targets as part of our corporate strategy and medium-term emissions reduction
targets of own operations (Scopes 1, 2, and 3 categories 1-14). Early 2026, we restated our corporate targets and cascaded to
business portfolios based on 2024 restated baseline. The targets and actions were established following the Science Based
Targets methodology for 2035. Our Climate and Environment Transition Plan covers short- and medium-term targets and
actions for our own operations and for our loan portfolio. For long term targets roadmap is planned to be developed as of 2032.
The plan describes our impacts from our investment activities as well as our and our financing activities´ impact on biodiversity,
describing our management approach. The Climate and Environment Transition Plan has been aligned with our Financial Plan,
including growth for new mortgages for highly energy efficient properties and corporate loans for renewable energy. The latest
version of our Climate and Environment Transition Plan was approved in February 2026.

Locked-in GHG emissions
We have established a forward-looking analysis of carbon related assets, based on TCFD definitions, that is reported to Board
on a quarterly basis. The emissions reduction of sectors is dependent on the companies’ transition plans and capabilities, which
influences if we meet our own decarbonisation targets, and drives our transition risk.

Challenges of climate targets and strategy implementation
A key challenge to delivering our climate strategy is our dependency on our customers to reduce their emissions, falling under
our Scope 3 category 15. Additional complexities arise from the current deregulation in EU, limited availability of data, and
uncertainty regarding the pace at which markets will adopt new technologies and practices. Further challenges include how
fast new energy efficient technologies and energy generation technologies can be deployed, how far regulation will make real
estate more energy efficient, and the decarbonisation of the electricity grid. We will support our customers through product
development.

To address these challenges, we have trained our customer-facing employees to understand, and be able to discuss with our
customers, sector-specific options for emissions abatement. We established sector-specific transition plan guidelines for our
customers in 2025 for sectors relevant for Luminor. These guidelines were developed using the insights gathered from the




                                                                                       Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025          51

=== pdf p.52 ===
sectoral analysis made during the C&E RBE analysis, the sector-specific guidelines from the Industry ESG Risk Management
Procedure, and market best practice. In 2026 we will continue building our transition planning capabilities, foster capability
building of our customers, and focus on possibilities for transition-related products development and structuring for corporate
customers

We have established an Industry ESG Risk Management Procedure that contains elements of sector transition guidance. During
2025, we completed the development of sector-based fact sheets for our relationship managers. In addition, we deepened the
analysis our retail mortgage and corporate loan portfolios and continued improving the availability, quality, and completeness
of our data, and of internal reporting.

We aim to align more closely our activities with the EU Taxonomy by increasing our data handling and processing capacity
according to the criteria set in the Taxonomy delegated acts and improve our reporting and automation capacity. We have
dedicated staff resources for this purpose, and planned expenditures on systems development.

We have considered the environmental, societal, and other developments in a range of climate scenarios to understand the
potential impacts on our portfolios, determine the timeline of the impacts, and potential risk mitigation approaches, including
decarbonisation to reduce transition risk. To assess the impact of C&E risks on our business environment, we applied data from
multiple climate scenarios, including SSP3-7.5, RCP 8.5, and RCP 6.0. Our decarbonisation development was informed by Net
Zero 2050, Below 2°C, Delayed Transition, and Current Policies scenarios and overarching purpose to limit global temperature
rise to 1.5°C. In revising our decarbonisation roadmap, we considered evolving national and EU policies, technological
advancements, and market developments.

Focus area 1 - Climate Risk Framework and Resilience
Impact and risk assessments
We assess climate and environmental risks to identify and manage physical and transition risks. We re-assessed these risks in
2025, include stress testing, and qualitative and quantitative analysis of acute physical risks, chronic changes, and transition
risks over the three time horizons. The results informed our strategic decisions, risk appetite, and mitigation strategies. The
processes we use to identify and assess our climate-related impacts and risks are described below in the respective sections
on: 'Analysis of the impact of climate and environmental risks on our business environment' (C&E RBE), 'Materiality assessment
for the impact of drivers of Climate and Environmental Risk on risk types' (C&E RMA), and are following IPCC guidance and
regulatory expectations. Results are integrated into our corporate strategy and disclosed in the Sustainability Statement and
Luminor Holding Pillar 3 Report 2025. Our analysis of our carbon-related assets identified corporate lending assets and business
activities that may need significant efforts to become compatible with the transition to a climate-neutral economy. These are
disclosed in the section 'Targets'.

Types of Climate and Environmental Risks assessed
Acute physical risks, and their consequences could damage the properties of our customers, or cause operational outages,
leading to financial losses. Long-term changes in climate and environmental conditions could cause damage to property and
both positive and negative fluctuations in the operational output of our customers. Transition risks may arise: in the short to
medium term from new regulations on emissions and resources, or on energy efficiency; in the medium term from a shift in
consumer preferences; and, in the medium to long term from the technological changes needed to adjust to a low-carbon
economy which may affect existing business models and hence the financial standing of our customers. Ultimately, these risks
may cause us losses if they are not assessed and mitigated promptly, or we may miss out on opportunities for financing the
transition. Businesses will need to adjust their operational strategies if they want to stay resilient. The C&E RBE assessment
described below screened whether our assets and business activities may be exposed to such physical or transition events. The
C&E RBE and the consecutive C&E RMA identified, assessed and quantified the extent to which assets and business activities
may be exposed to, and are sensitive to, the physical risk drivers or transition events identified.

Methodology and Data Sources
In 2025 we updated our methodology and analysis and concluded that Baltic countries face a similar set of principal physical
and transition risks, except for environmental regulatory frameworks which differ in each country.

The 2025 C&E RBE and C&E RMA included climate-related scenario analysis, using data from various climate scenarios The final
C&E RBE assessment was based on a comprehensive review of regulations, analysis of relevant publications, and internal
expertise. The severity of the impact of the drivers of physical risk and the frequency of change in them was assessed
qualitatively, over various time horizons, following the regional climate projections of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate
Change (IPCC) and guidance from the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report together with the guidance notes on the IPCC Fifth
Assessment Report. We assessed transitional risks using publicly available reliable data.

The data in the C&E RBE process was linked to climate scenarios through the Climate and Environmental Risk assessment (CERA)
which identifies the critical areas, specific impacts, and tailored strategic responses for our operations. CERA guides our
prioritisation of Climate Risk Stress Testing in the credit portfolio, and it focuses on key economic activities or risk drivers. The
C&E RMA and the risk quantification processes are informed by the outcomes of the C&E RBE, and the results of the C&E RMA
and the stress testing informed the development of the risk appetite metrics in our Financial Plan.

Analysis of the impact of climate and environmental risks on our business environment
In 2025, we updated our Procedure for C&E RBE analysis. This analysis has three parts; identification of climate and
environmental risks, business environment scan (BES), which provides understanding of transition risks and other risks arising
from various aspects of the business environment in which we operate, and the CERA, which evaluates the scale of the impact
of climate and environmental risk drivers on main portfolios, economic sectors and for each Baltic country separately, and
recommends risk mitigation measures by business areas and industry sectors.

In 2025 our C&E RBE assessment focused on customer lending. C&E RBE is also considered relevant for Pensions, Discretionary
Portfolio Management, Treasury, and Markets because of the nature and scope of their activities and the regulations that govern




                                                                                         Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025          55

=== pdf p.56 ===
associated processes. These business areas can apply the analysis results for their area-specific assessments. We assessed the
impact of climate and environmental risk drivers, separately for retail mortgages, private leasing and corporate lending over the
three time horizons.

We assessed physical climate and environmental risks at NUTS3 level within a medium time horizon. The results revealed varying
levels of risk across the Baltic NUTS3 regions for certain C&E risks such as river flooding or water stress. while other C&E risks,
for example, heatwaves or coastal erosion were found to be the same.

The physical risks for private customers, include changing weather, coastal erosion, and soil degradation, with mitigation
measures such as insurance and collateral assessments. There, we must engage in proactive risk management together with
our customers, make strategic adjustments, and adhere to evolving regulatory expectations for mitigation of climate and
environmental risk.

The physical and transitional risk assessment for businesses revealed different risk drivers and impacts for different economic
sectors. In the short term all customers will face policy, litigation, and reputational risks and customers in several sectors will
face as well include chronic and acute physical risks, which may impact financial flows and collateral. Accordingly, sectors need
to be considered separately with tailored transition plans.

Risk Materiality assessment of ESG Risk Drivers impact on Risk Types
We performed an annual Risk Materiality Assessment (RMA) Process to evaluate the impact of ESG Risk Drivers on Risk Types
defined in our Risk Taxonomy. This process evaluates how ESG risks may impact credit, market, liquidity, operational,
compliance and other risk types using scenario analysis and expert judgment. Key risk materiality assessment criteria are
financial materiality threshold and non-financial risk grid defined in our Risk Policy. More details are available in Luminor Holding
Pillar 3 Report 2025.

In 2025, we expanded the RMA methodology from C&E RMA to ESG RMA, to cover not only Environmental (including Climate)
Risk Drivers but also Social and Governance risk drivers in our Risk Materiality Assessment (RMA) processes. We also integrated
the RMA process with DMA by mapping all identified risk outcomes from the DMA process, the IROs, to our risk taxonomy and
main risk types. In 2026, we plan to further integrate DMA and RMA processes.

Resilience analysis
We evaluate the resilience of our strategy and business model to climate change for both short term capital adequacy
assessment (3 years) and medium to long-term climate scenario stress testing (10-25 years). The assessment leverages on the
existing ICAAP framework.

Climate risk drivers are treated as amplifiers of existing risk types and are considered under both normative and economic
perspectives, including stress testing and sensitivity analysis. The results conclude that in the short term, our management
buffers are adequate to absorb climate risk related shocks under different scenarios.

The long-term climate stress test, based on NGFS scenarios over 10–25+ years, assesses business model resilience, highlights
more climate sensitive sectors and supports strategic portfolio steering. These scenarios assume a gradual economic transition,
a shift toward lower carbon energy systems and technology deployment aligned with recognized scientific pathways. The results
show that climate risk-related impacts may increase but remain manageable through ongoing transition planning and portfolio
adjustments. Estimated financial effects from material climate risks, as well as mitigation actions, are incorporated into
transition planning.

Stewardship and Capacity Building
In 2025, we continued to raise customers and employee’s awareness about climate change and environmental risk management,

In 2025, we launched our first corporate customer ESG newsletter, to share insights, tools, and best practices that help

to climate and environmental change, we will continue hosting seminars on how these factors impact businesses, fostering
understanding and informed action and issue our customer newsletter on a regular basis...

We will continue rolling out transition planning tools, including abatement lever libraries, transition planning guidance, and
initiate customer engagement for C&E risk mitigation with the support of transition advisors. Our goal is to establish dedicated
customer advisory capability to: engage customers on setting and improving targets and transition plans; support Climate and
Environment risk and materiality assessments; analyse ESG due diligence and risk ratings; and recommend mitigation and
improvement actions. We are building the advisors' capabilities to be able to engage with customers on C&E risk and risk
mitigation measures, such as transition planning, related trainings and guidance to customers. We will also continue to work
with local governments and banking associations to develop solutions for local climate data and the future projections.

Focus area 3 - Climate risk management of Financing and Investment Portfolios
C&E Risk Integration into Loan Origination and Monitoring Processes
We follow a risk-based approach, documented in our ESG Risk Assessment Procedure. We integrate the result of the
assessment into our credit decision-making process for legal entity customers. Initially we evaluate a customer's inherent
environmental and climate risk level, using industry risk classification, transition risk heatmap, and existence of existing and/or
historical negative ESG risk event check. For inherently high-risk customers we conduct detailed risk assessments, and residual
ESG risk levels are recorded in credit documentation. We use an exclusion list to ensure compliance with sustainability and
ethical standards, maintain sector-specific guidance for industries with elevated ESG risks, and apply climate risk assessments
for mortgage lending, focusing on the energy efficiency performance of the collateral and assessment of flood risk.

In 2025, we enhanced the procedure for ESG risk assessments for SMEs and large corporate customers. We continued to collect
climate and environmental risk data from our largest corporate customers, as part of our ESG risk rating., and gathered
preliminary information about mitigation and targets for reducing environmental impacts. We also enhanced the data we collect
from registers.

Looking ahead, in 2026 we plan to explore automation of customer due diligence and continue integration of climate risk
assessments based on risk data into Loan Origination and Monitoring processes.

Our financed emissions decreased even as the corporate lending portfolio increased, primarily due to a reallocation toward
sectors with lower emission intensity, improvements in customers’ financial performance, and enhanced data availability. In the
mortgages and motor vehicles portfolios, emissions declined, driven by a higher share of energy‑efficient buildings and electric
or hybrid vehicles, supported by continued improvements in data quality. Data methodologies and limitations are provided
below.

Each year we assess the exposure of our credit portfolio to environmental risks, both transitional and physical risks using the
EBRD industry classification. This assessment found high-risk assets in our portfolio that are linked to high levels of energy and
emission intensity and classified 17.3% in 2025 compared to 17.9% in 2024 of our corporate loans as linked to high levels of
energy and emission intensity and therefore exposed to high inherent environmental risk. In the risk assessment, loans with
sustainable purpose and loans to companies owned by local governments that have committed to net zero targets and have
transition plans in place are excluded from the high‑risk classification, irrespective of their sectoral risk profile.

Exclusions and risk limits
To limit our exposure to high-risk customers and assets, and to support the transition of the energy sector, we have in place
the exclusion list of our Sustainability Policy to exclude power generation from coal, thermal coal mining, and extraction of oil
and oil shale if the company concerned has not committed to net zero by 2050 or earlier and does not have a transition plan in
place, or will not make that commitment and have a transition plan within 12 months after the financing agreement is signed. In
2025, to strengthen climate and biodiversity considerations we restricted financing energy generation, and production of energy
products made from peat, aligning with our biodiversity focus and peatland restoration initiatives.

We also have in place risk appetite metrics for the mortgage portfolio for financing real estate with a low energy efficiency
profile and high climate risk sectors exposure.

Transition risk reduction through customer' s transition planning
We continued to require our largest corporate customers operating in high Environmental risk sectors to demonstrate their
actions to reduce their environmental impact by requesting them to have transition plans and where appropriate to calculate

their emissions and set targets for reducing their carbon emissions intensity as defined in our ESG Risk Assessment Procedure.
We also updated our Industry ESG Risk Management Procedure, which gives industry-specific guidance on the main ESG risks
and the key elements of transition planning and risk mitigation for customers active in these sectors. In 2025, new lending
volume to customers in high climate-risk sectors that have transition plans in place reached 75%, short of our 90% target as
customers adjusted their plans to changes in CSRD. The transitional plan definition and contextual information are disclosed in

In 2025, we strengthened our transition planning capabilities to support customers in adapting to a low-carbon economy. We
introduced sector-specific transition plan guidelines and developed carbon abatement libraries for key industries. To deepen

Steering credit financing to lower carbon facilities
We continued to offer EIB-backed financing to improve access to finance for small and medium-sized enterprises and
strengthen the Baltic region’s transition toward a low-carbon economy. We also continued to offer financing aligned with EBRD
requirements for lower-carbon energy projects, energy-efficient real estate and development of renewable energy projects
and increased by 68% compared to 2024 and reached 305.0 million EUR of financing for the period 2021-2025, reaching our
2027 target already by the end of 2025.

We increased the share of mortgage lending exposures in our portfolio that are for housing with an EPC of A or better to 32.8%
in 2025 compared to 28.9% in 2024. We will continue taking additional action in 2026 to reach our emission reduction targets
by financing new real estate projects classed A or higher, and by integrating environmental into our lending strategy and decision
making.

We improved the availability and collection of data on mortgage collateral, like their EPC and primary energy demand. For retail
lending, we identified and assessed the physical climate risks in our markets following the EU taxonomy classification, with flood,
coastal erosion, heatwave and drought risks found to be the most material for real estate, and we used climate change risk
maps to identify properties in areas that are at risk of acute damage from climate change.

Assets Under Management
We intend to reduce the climate impact of our assets under management activities as part of our ESG targets. Our Sustainable
Investment Guidelines describe how we incorporate sustainability risk (into investment decisions associated with the
Discretionary Portfolio Management (DPM) and pension funds managed by Asset Management Subsidiaries.

Our DPM business continued to consider climate change a priority issue in 2025, favouring investments with better indicators
on climate-related PAI considering all else is equal. As a result, we made progress with multiple climate-related PAI indicators,

When on-boarding new customers, we assess their sustainability preferences.

Integrating sustainability risk, is important as well for our Asset Management Subsidiaries in providing competitive 2nd and 3rd

time significantly reducing investments in the fossil fuel sector and in companies involved in controversial activities.

Data Methodologies and limitations:
For our assessment of greenhouse gas emissions, we used operational control boundaries as per the GHG protocol and market
practice, with no significant changes to emissions accounting inventory scope as compared to previous year. We excluded non-
material categories (e.g., upstream/downstream transportation, franchises, end-of-life product treatment), because of limited
use of products, limited significance to our operations, or limited estimated significance on the total emission. Our Scope 3
inventory includes emissions from paper use (Category 1), IT equipment (Category 2), waste generated (Category 5), business
travel (Category 6), and employee commuting (Category 7). Additionally, we are calculating emissions for Category 15 related to
lending products and investments.

Own operations emissions
To evaluate the performance and effectiveness of climate change related impact risks and opportunities in our own operations,
we measure our carbon footprint in tCO2e, calculated as per our Instruction for Luminor Own Emission Data Collection. We
assess the accuracy of own emission sustainability reporting data as reasonable based on the sources used for estimations. Our
data and calculations are validated by our external assurance provided according to limited assurance scope.

To calculate our Scope 1 emissions, we used Republic of Estonia's GHG emission footprint calculator for organisations, using
average emission factors for fuels used. For Scope 2 emission calculations in location-based calculations and market-based
calculations, where no contractual instruments are in place, we use the Association of Issuing Bodies (AIB) emission factors for
electricity and heat energy.

The energy consumption data we report is based on invoices we receive from the landlords of our facilities, some of which use
square metres of floor space to approximate our share of total heat energy or electricity consumption. In 2025, no external
solution was used to manage our energy consumption data. Energy consumption is an aggregate of the electricity and heating
energy that we use in our facilities. Electricity consumption is reported to us in units of energy consumed. In some facilities,
where heat energy consumption as units of energy consumed is not provided in the invoices, we calculate the heat energy
consumption from the monetary value invoiced and monthly heat energy tariff in the respective municipality.

We have renewable energy contracts with renewable energy certificates of origin as contractual instruments in place for
purchased electricity. The contractual instruments cover 73.6% of electricity emissions and 66.3% of total energy related
(Scope 2) emissions. For heat energy we do not have any contractual instruments in place.

Scope 3 emissions are calculated for material categories as per the assessment we made at the end of 2023. Most of the Scope
3 emissions are calculated using primary data, such as travelled distance, purchased amount (pieces) or weight. Where such
data is not available, spend-based estimations are applied. For estimation of employee commuting, we extrapolate data
received from questionnaires to cover all employees, using country averages, with adjustments made for time away from the
office. Additionally, if the respondent has said, that during 2025 they were out of office for more than 6 weeks, it was assumed
that the time spent out of office was 10 weeks

For various Scope 3 emissions - generated waste (category 5), business travel (category 6) related to employee transportation,
where service provider data is not available, and for hotel stays, employee commute (category 7) - we use average country
emission factors developed by the Republic of Estonia. Scope 3 financed emissions (Category 15) are calculated according to




62           Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025

=== pdf p.63 ===
the PCAF methodology, including PCAF provided emission factor data base. For paper use (category 1) GHG emission
estimations we use emission factors for Baltic countries provided by Climatiq.

For emissions calculated for IT equipment (category 2) manufacturer emission reports were used, deducting the use phase
emissions provided in the manufacturer emission report. Where such emission reports are not available, we apply spend-based
emission estimations. During 2025 we improved data accuracy for the emissions accruing from purchased IT equipment.

For the waste amount estimations for Lithuania, we apply waste weight per employee from Latvia. In Estonia precise waste
amounts are provided for

The primary data used for the Scope 1 emissions in 2024 and 2025 made up 100%, and for Scope 2 it made 100.0% in both years.
For Scope 3 primary data use made up 59.6%, excluding Category 15, while in 2025 primary data use for Scope 3 made up 64.0%,
excluding Category 15.

GHG removals
We use the MoorFutures standard to quantify greenhouse gas (GHG) removals and calculate reduction in emissions. The
standard is designed for projects that rewet drained peatlands in the temperate climate zone, The MoorFutures methodology
has been adjusted for Baltic conditions by the Foundation for Peatland Restoration and Conservation and uses a forward-
looking baseline scenario to estimate emissions reductions from peatland rewetting projects.

Emissions in the project scenario are calculated from the expected changes in water levels and vegetation using the GEST
approach or other approved quantification methods. Potential carbon sinks are excluded and a methane peak after rewetting
is included. Data limitations include the challenge of accurately estimating nitrous oxide emissions and peat depletion rates
over long time horizons. This is addressed by excluding nitrous oxide and excluding areas where peat is projected to deplete
within 100 years. The approach is designed overall to provide a robust but conservative quantification of the climate benefits
from peatland restoration. Laboratory of Flora and Geobotany has performed an evaluation of the rewetted peatland conditions
and the restoration measures.

The Foundation for Peatland Restoration and Conservation reports the emissions removed to us on an annual basis. There is
no additional external validation.

Scope 3 - financed emissions
We use PCAF methodology for calculating financed emissions. PCAF methodology has been developed and is being used by
multiple industries, there are flaws that require workarounds such as missing emissions factors for various asset types. We have
included all absolute financed emissions for all relevant asset classes or sectors covered in PCAF Plan A and justified any
exclusions.

Motor vehicles financed emissions
Motor vehicle finance emissions cover vehicles from corporate and private customers and include collaterals with an engine
that can be driven, flown, or sailed, but exclude collaterals that are considered as machinery but not considered as movable
property. All vehicles GHG emissions data is based on PCAF emissions factors and average kilometres driven data. No actual
data for GHG emissions has been used in this calculation. Rather, we have made the following assumptions: we use the PCAF
database where if a vehicle doesn’t wholly match a type provided by PCAF, it is mapped to the closest possible type considering
way of transportation and approximate engine size; and, for kilometres driven an average of kilometres driven, from national
statistics, is used. For more specialised vehicles national statistics are extrapolated should they be unavailable.

We used proxies for motor vehicles financed emissions: Emission factor may come from multiple sources; PCAF emission factors
were provided for the majority of motor vehicles based on their fuel type and/or model and manufacturer; additional emission
factors are estimated for Railway transport, airplanes and vessels, for which PCAF database doesn’t provide an emission factor.
Vehicle loans financed emissions of on-balance sheet assets do not reconcile with financial reporting as financed emissions
includes only drivable vehicles. In addition, on-balance sheet assets may have double entries caused by duplicate entries for
vehicles in registries.




                                                                                      Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025        63

=== pdf p.64 ===
The resulting accuracy of sustainability reporting data for motor vehicles financed emissions can be assessed reasonable based
on the type of data and sources used for the estimations (vehicle model and manufacturer, average distance travelled, country
and vehicle type). In the future, we plan to use actual emissions based on the extracts from local vehicle registries and rely on
the gradual improvement of the vehicle type data in the registries and national statistics.

Mortgage portfolio financed emissions
Our mortgage portfolio EPC rating is based on mapping immovable collateral to PCAF database using collateral type mapping.
If we were not able to map collateral to the database, we exclude the contract from EPC reporting and added to the 'business
loans' financed emissions calculation. In the majority of cases this includes machinery and equipment mortgages. For collaterals
with real or estimated EPC rating, financed emissions are calculated based on PCAF quality score 3 using the EPC rating to align
emission factor.

We make the following assumptions for mortgage financed emissions: for collateral types available in our systems, in case they
do not match fully with the types available in PCAF database, we implemented a manual collateral mapping; and immovable
properties that should not be emitting any GHG emissions, such as plots of land we exclude from the mapping.

We used the following proxies for mortgage financed emissions: All GHG emission factors are provided from PCAF database;
EPC ratings are sourced from external registries, when data is noted down as 'Real' EPC rating or is estimated based on a
collateral's year of construction or reconstruction and noted down as 'Estimated' EPC rating; if PCAF score 5 is calculated, and
when the size in square meters of property is not available, we use collateral type dwelling and assume that 1 collateral is being
financed.

Mortgage loans financed emissions on-balance sheet assets does not reconcile with financial reporting due, in the main to
methodological differences relating to collateral allocations and typology. Several loans may be backed by several collaterals,
of which some collaterals do not classify for emissions accounting such as land plots or non-heated buildings such as garages.

The resulting accuracy of sustainability reporting data for mortgage portfolio's financed emissions has been assessed 'sufficient'
based on the sources used for the emission factor estimations and collateral type information in banking systems. We aim to
improve the data accuracy by updating missing data elements to ensure required data availability for the existing portfolio in
the banking systems in all three Baltic countries.

Corporate lending financed emissions
Emissions calculations for corporate lending includes business loans of all corporate customers, excluding Motor vehicles which
are included in Motor vehicles asset class calculations.

Financed emissions calculations for business loans depend on collateral type. For business loans secured by commercial real
estate, collateral financed emissions are calculated based on real or estimated EPC data, if it is not available, emissions are
calculated as per PCAF standard describing quality scores 4 and 5, basing calculations on immovable property's floor area or
dwelling year. Commercial real-estate collaterals are selected based on preselected collateral types that have been mapped
to PCAF provided collateral type list. If commercial real estate does not comply with the preselected collateral type list, financed
emissions are calculated as per business loans requirements. For business loans financed emissions calculations depend on
financial information availability, NACE code, and country of jurisdiction. On business loans level PCAF uses Exiobase segregation
that directly can be correlated to industry NACE codes. For some of industry NACE codes PCAF emission factors for Baltics
were missing. As a result, emissions for a non-material part of corporate portfolio have not been calculated. Additionally, for
NACE Code D.35.30, more generic sector emissions factors have been used following PCAF recommendation.

Corporate loans financed emissions on-balance sheet assets does not reconcile with financial reporting as financed emissions
reporting excludes guarantees and cash cards (as methodology is not provided by PCAF) and bonds. Emissions include types of
leasing other than vehicle leasing (which is accounted for under the vehicle financed emissions).

The resulting accuracy of sustainability reporting data for corporate portfolio's financed emissions has been assessed sufficient
based on the sources used for the emission factors, collateral type information and companies’ financial data availability in
banking systems. We plan to improve the data accuracy by working together with the local banking associations to increase the




64     Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025

=== pdf p.65 ===
coverage of the primary energy demand and EPC data of buildings in local registries. The data quality is also expected to improve
gradually as we plan to collect more data from companies published CSRD reports and our ESG data collection questionnaires
on real emissions.

Listed and unlisted equity and corporate bonds
The unlisted bonds and equity asset class includes all on-balance sheet equity investments in businesses, non-profits, and any
other structure of organisation that are not traded on a market and are for general corporate purposes. Calculations for
financed emission were made according to PCAF data quality score 5 requirements. With limited data about emissions for
scopes 1, 2 and 3, the emissions were calculated using our exposure and emission factors provided by the PCAF emission factor
database. Since the database lacked data on emission factors for emissions divided by assets for a sector, we used PCAF method
3c to calculate financed emissions.

The listed bonds asset class includes all on-balance sheet listed corporate bonds that are traded on a market and are for
general corporate purposes. Financed emissions for the absolute Scope 1 and 2 and financed emissions of Scope 3 were
calculated according to PCAF data quality score 1 requirements, using the data from latest available consolidated annual reports
of the financed company. GHG emissions data was available, but in some cases enterprise value including cash (EVIC) had to
calculated or substituted with appropriate value. The substitutions were made using available data on market capitalisation,
equity and liabilities, income statements or other available financial data found in the consolidated annual financial report. Data
for all calculations came from the financed companies latest consolidated annual report, either 2025 or if unavailable then from
2024 or 2023.

The resulting accuracy of sustainability reporting data can be assessed sufficient based on the sources used for the emission
and companies consolidated financial reports.

Sovereign debt
This asset class includes sovereign bonds and sovereign loans issued in domestic or foreign currencies. Financed emissions are
calculated based on PCAF Plan A standard according to data quality Score 1 or Score 2 requirements. Source for GDP_PPP is
World Bank Group and for the GHG emissions UN data from Greenhouse Gas Inventory Data. PCAF does not provide emission
factors individually for Scope 1, 2, and 3 of the assets and therefore only aggregate total emissions have been disclosed.

The resulting accuracy of sustainability reporting data can be assessed sufficient based on the sources used for the emission
factors. Currently, we do not have any plans to improve the data quality and look forward to the gradual improvement of the
emission factors by the UN.

Biodiversity and ecosystems
Our primary exposure to biodiversity-related risks stems from financed activities and suppliers operating in or near
biodiversity‑sensitive areas such as Natura 2000 sites or peatland ecosystems. These activities may lead to degradation of
natural habitats and disturbance of protected species, particularly in designated conservation zones. Sectors such as
agriculture and forestry present elevated risks due to their dependence on ecosystem services and use of inputs. Conversely,
we operate exclusively from facilities located in urban areas. The Exploring Natural Capital Opportunities, Risks and Exposure
(ENCORE) and Key Biodiversity Areas mapping of our facilities gave low or very low materiality assessment ratings, meaning our
own operations do not have material biodiversity impacts or do not affect areas that are sensitive for biodiversity.
