In 2025, we advanced how we identify and assess actual and potential impacts on biodiversity and ecosystems across our own
operations and value chain. Building on our work in 2024 we implemented the Partnership for Biodiversity Accounting Financials
(PBAF) Standard to guide a more structured and decision-useful assessment.

For our value chain, we conducted a portfolio-wide screening of biodiversity dependencies and impacts, with a focus on sectors
with high nature-related risk dependencies such as agriculture and forestry, with an analysis of ecosystem service
dependencies, such as water, soil, and pollination, and pressures such as land use change, pollution, and resource extraction.
The Analysis of Impact of C&E RBE in 2025, supported this by evaluating environmental risks across the three time horizons.

Subject matter experts and material topic owners used these insights to define and assess biodiversity-related IROs, as
documented in the sections Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) and Sustainability Reporting Processes and stakeholder
perspectives were integrated through our engagement activities, detailed in the section Stakeholder Engagement.

Our criteria for assessing IROs are described in the section 'IRO Assessment and Sustainability Reporting Processes' and include
ecosystem services that have been, or may be, disrupted. Transition and physical risks related to biodiversity and ecosystems
have been identified and assessed in scope of the C&E RBE. We assess systemic biodiversity and ecosystem risks using the
ENCORE database, which highlights potential large-scale disruptions to ecosystem services such as soil degradation. We
evaluate these risks for their potential financial impact and complement this with ClimCycle data and sector-level biodiversity
impact metrics to identify cross-sector vulnerabilities and systemic exposure.

POLICIES
Biodiversity‑related material impacts, risks, and opportunities were identified across our own operations, suppliers, and
financed activities in scope of the 2025 DMA and the process confirmed the continued materiality of biodiversity. Our existing
policies and due diligence processes are used to address and manage the material biodiversity‑related IROs. Our commitment
to biodiversity protection is embedded in our Sustainability Policy and operationalised through the ESG Due Diligence Standard.
Material biodiversity impacts are addressed via ESG due diligence processes, including the ESG Risk Assessment Procedure.
These processes consider risks such as proximity to protected areas, species disturbance, and ecosystem degradation. Risk
treatment mechanisms — such as avoidance, mitigation, or engagement — are defined accordingly and supported by ESG risk
assessment questionnaires and adverse media screening tools, which flag biodiversity-related controversies during enhanced




66      Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025

=== pdf p.67 ===
due diligence. These measures integrate biodiversity considerations into credit decisions, supplier engagement, and
sustainability reporting.

In addition, our policies apply exclusion rules to prevent harm to high conservation value areas, differentiate between physical
and transition risks, and address sustainable land use and regenerative agriculture practices. The policies require risk
assessments and transition plans for high-risk sectors. In 2025, we added deforestation risk minimisation to our Sustainability
policy and intend in 2026 to integrate deforestation provisions into our due diligence processes. A further description of the
policies is provided in section 'Our policies, procedure and standards' of the 'Notes to the sustainability statement'.

TARGETS
Biodiversity target setting is planned once data quality and methodologies are sufficiently mature. An action plan for target
setting and biodiversity risk management with 2026 milestones is embedded in our Climate and Environmental Transition Plan.
In 2025, we started to assess nature dependencies to establish a baseline and explore ways to reduce impacts and resource
dependencies across operations and customers by 2028.

We finalized the biodiversity impact assessment at the end of 2025 and initiated a focused analysis of key impact metrics to
guide future monitoring, with particular attention to agriculture and forestry sectors where biodiversity considerations are
critical.

In 2024, we committed to establishing quantified biodiversity targets once robust data on our dependencies and impacts
became available. While we made progress in understanding these dimensions in 2025, we did not set formal targets due to the
need for greater confidence in data quality and methodologies, as well as the development of processes to monitor and
influence biodiversity impacts — particularly at loan origination and monitoring stages. We will revisit target setting once further
maturity is achieved in these areas.

In 2026, we plan to review the integration of biodiversity considerations in credit decision-making. This includes enhancing due
diligence tools with biodiversity-related questions and developing nature-related risk and impact indicators for portfolio-level
insights. In addition, we aim to engage in knowledge building activities for our customers, especially those operating in the
agriculture sector.

ACTIONS
In 2025, we advanced our understanding of nature related impacts and dependencies and integrated additional nature-related
risk drivers into our risk assessment processes - the Analysis of Climate and Environmental risks on our business environment
for lending portfolios and the DMA process. We analysed the requirements of nature impacts and dependencies accounting
methodology of PBAF standard and performed the related analysis of our loan portfolio using the ENCORE database. This
analysis identified material dependencies and pressures on ecosystem services, particularly within the agriculture sector, and
confirmed that biodiversity-related risks - especially those linked to crop and animal production - meet the materiality
threshold defined in our Risk Policy and Risk Management Framework. We finalised the biodiversity impact assessment and
initiated an analysis of key impact metrics to guide future monitoring efforts, with particular attention to agriculture and forestry
sectors.

In 2025, we developed sector one-pagers based on our Industry ESG risk management procedure, which provides
agriculture‑specific ESG risk guidance for Relationship Managers, including activity based environmental risk levels (e.g.,
livestock farming) and expectations for mitigation such as reduced fertiliser use, regenerative farming practices and soil and
water stewardship, ensures that biodiversity impacts and risks are systematically assessed and addressed through client
engagement and credit decisions applying risk based approach. In addition, we developed transition guidelines for agriculture
sector that Relationship Managers can use in their discussions with the customers to guide them in transition planning.

We integrated the biodiversity related commitments and actions into our Climate and Environmental Transition plan including
the integration of additional questions into the agriculture sector specific due diligence tool.

Transition plan on biodiversity and ecosystems
We strengthened our Climate and Environment Transition Plan by integrating biodiversity-related physical, transition, and
systemic risks. Our biodiversity risks resilience is assessed through the inclusion of biodiversity in our DMA, ESG Risk Assessment
Procedure, and sector-level analysis using ENCORE data. We quantified nature-related dependencies across sub-sectors and
evaluated potential financial risks, including reputational impacts stemming from biodiversity loss. These insights inform our
strategy, risk limits, and follow-up actions, as outlined in the “Climate Change chapter. In our 2025 DMA, nature was considered
a silent stakeholder, and biodiversity-related IRO assessments were guided by scientific literature and sectoral publications.
Stakeholder involvement is detailed in the “Stakeholder Engagement” section, which explains how external perspectives were
incorporated into the identification and assessment process. Our resilience analysis focuses on financial materiality across our
lending and investment portfolios. It is conducted through two core processes: the Analysis of Impact of C&E RBE, which covers
all customer segments, and the DMA, which includes in portfolio assessment and quantification analysis both retail mortgage
and corporate lending portfolios as well as investment and pensions portfolios. Risks and opportunities related to biodiversity
and ecosystems are assessed for lending portfolio at sector level using ENCORE data. Impacts and risks from own operations
are deemed immaterial.

Resource use and circular economy
PROGRESS AND UPDATES SINCE LAST REPORT
Resource use and circular economy topic is not material for the current reporting period, and information is provided for
context, continuity and transparency purposes only. Efficient resource use and the transition toward circular business models
remain important themes in the broader sustainability landscape. While circularity principles, such as waste reduction, reuse,
and responsible product design, continue to support long-term decarbonisation and resilience, their direct financial materiality
within our own operations remains limited due to our service-based, non-resource-intensive business model. However,
circularity measures are increasingly relevant in the context of our financing activities.

As part of our commitment to decarbonising the loan portfolio and achieving net zero by 2050, we recognise the role of circular
economy principles in strengthening client resilience and supporting the shift toward more sustainable business models. We
will continue to monitor developments in this area and integrate relevant practices where they support our broader
sustainability objectives.

SOCIAL INFORMATION
Customers and end users
Our strategy and business model are aligned with our commitment to meet the evolving needs of and provide value to our
customers which we manage by customer segment. We are here to improve the financial health of our customers and our
home markets, and to support their growth, to ensure mutual success and long-term sustainability by ensuring our value
proposition relevance to our customers. We have dedicated customer service roles in place to strengthen our customer
relationships, understand customer needs and increase customer satisfaction.

Our strategy recognises that specific customer segments have unique needs. To younger customers, we promote financial
literacy and responsible decision-making, for older customers we provide non-digital access to our service supported by
consultations, while for customers with disabilities, we provide enhanced accessibility to our facilities and digital offerings.

POLICIES
We focus on transparency, accountability, and remediation to ensure an ethical and customer-oriented approach. We strive to
satisfy our customers, as well as respect their fundamental human rights by providing fair and honest treatment that does not
discriminate and offering good service.

We manage material impacts of our products on customers through our Sustainability Policy, which promotes adherence to the
UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, OECD Guidelines, and ILO standards. We identify following human rights
topics relevant to customers (right to information, right to equality & non-discrimination, right to effective remedy and right to
protection from harmful business impacts) and uphold their rights to clear and accurate information through personalized,
multi-channel communication, timely updates on legal terms and pricing, and responsiveness to inquiries. Advanced feedback
mechanisms help us tailor engagement strategies to evolving needs.

Our Luminor guide to a memorable customer experience (“the Guide”) requires offers to be based on customer needs,
supported by daily service quality assessments to notice early signs of lack of competence, and act accordingly. Lending




                                                                                                Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025   69

=== pdf p.70 ===
practices consider affordability and risk tolerance, guided by the Lending Risk Parameters for Private Individuals Procedure.
We raise our customers awareness of financial literacy by providing regular newsletters covering such topics as fraud schemes,
pension funds 'performance, and financial market overviews.

We strive to make our services accessible to all customers without discrimination and ensure fair treatment. Our Code of
Conduct defines core values, while the Guide sets professional requirements for employees, including support for customers
with special needs, reinforced through regular training. The Guide was updated during 2025 to enhance accessibility related
provisions, before assisting, adaptive communication style and allowing extra time.

We ensure customers’ right to remedy through the Customer Complaints, Feedback and Requests Handling Procedure, which
we updated in 2025 to improve definitions and resolution timing. After a customer submits a complaint, we notify them
immediately that we will respond within 15 calendar days. The employee responsible for handling the complaint evaluates the
situation, gathers all issue-related information, and provides a solution to the customer, including compensation if applicable.
Feedback is used to mitigate negative outcomes from process deficiencies, human error, fraud attempts, or technical incidents.

Following our ESG Due Diligence Standard, we address human rights in customer operations through a risk-based approach in
our due diligence process. For large corporate clients in high-risk industries, we use questionnaires to assess social and
governance risks, and compliance with international standards. Results inform mitigation capacity and residual risk, which are
documented and considered in credit decisions.

TARGETS
We have established targets, metrics and actions to address the identified material IROs. The metrics established reflect key
factors such as customer satisfaction, transparency, accountability, and remediation, which collectively drive the quality of
customer relationships. All the targets are reviewed as part of our annual strategy review process in engagement with all relevant
internal stakeholders.

ACTIONS
The relevance of our operations to customers is ensured and evaluated through continuous engagement with them. We engage
with customers and stakeholders in a number of ways including regular satisfaction surveys, mystery shopping, focus groups,
and our annual ESG Business Materiality Assessment Insights from these engagements are integrated into decision-making to
ensure our products and services remain accessible, responsive, and aligned with customer needs.

We consistently measure customer satisfaction to follow up our quality of services, to capture all early signals of imperfections
and to collect call to actions for improvements. Both retail and corporate customer satisfaction is measured through NPS
surveys, complemented by Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT) and sentiment tracking for digital channels. Customers are
invited to provide feedback on their overall experience in our biannual NPS survey, from which we calculate a NPS score.
Throughout the year, customers also provide feedback on their most recent interaction, from which we calculate the
transactional NPS score. Our Customer Experience Unit follows up with customers who gave an NPS score between 0 and 8 to

understand their experience and address any unresolved issues. We continued to focus on service quality and personalised
communication. Mystery shopping and updated service standards improved transactional NPS.

In 2025, we tracked effectiveness through feedback surveys, and improved consultations and engagement. We are continuing
to improve the quality of our consultation through regular quality assessments and proactive engagement with dormant
customers, and by keeping relationships balanced from the risk perspective and understanding how to create more value from
banking with us. We ran dedicated training of the Guide, with a focusing on customer retention, professionalism, and CRM usage.

We improved our service quality and hence our customer relationships using mystery shoppers and updated service guidelines
to enhance personal experience across channels. Annual independent Service quality survey of financial sector recorded higher
ratings of our sales and onsite service consultation channels. We expanded quality assessments to all channels, with weekly
measurements and regular reporting. An annual ESG business materiality assessment also supports our customer service
strategy described in the section 'General disclosures'.

Due to competitive and commercial sensitivity, the disclosure intentionally focuses on high‑level actions and processes rather
than detailed descriptions of digital functionalities or implementation specifics.

To identify what action is needed and appropriate in response to identified risk we apply a continuous, multi‑channel assessment
process described above. Using mystery shoppers and customer satisfaction tools we are able to identify customer emerging
needs and tackle early signs of customer experience and to initiate the activities for improvements. In addition, during the year
we enhanced our offerings by adding new functionalities and products. We also updated our complaint-handling procedures in
2025. Operational risk reports now include data on complaints requesting financial compensation to identify root causes and
implement mitigation plans. We are improving the efficiency if our IT systems in 2026. We improved our communication with
customers during complaint investigations by implementing service level agreements and providing interim notifications. We
maintain close cooperation with local regulators and follow their recommendations. The outcomes of these processes are
systematically integrated into decision‑making to determine improvements to our digital and physical accessibility, update
service standards, enhance product functionalities, refine consultation quality, strengthen complaint‑handling procedures, and
inform targeted customer communication.

In 2025, we continued the implementation of the action plan to improve digital and physical accessibility and executed trainings.
Following a third-party accessibility audit, we implemented improvements to ensue better accessibility across our digital
channels. To improve customer experience, we analysed the customer feedback from NPS surveys and customer complaints.
The identified gaps in customer experience in digital channels were addressed both in 2025 and will be part of our plans for
further improvements 2026.

GOVERNANCE INFORMATION
PROGRESS AND UPDATES SINCE LAST REPORT
Business conduct
Business conduct topic is not material for the current reporting period, and information is provided for context, continuity and
transparency purposes only. Our Code of Conduct continues to set clear expectations for ethical behaviour, supported by
internal controls and ESG due diligence applied to all new third parties. We also reassess regularly key partners to ensure
alignment with our principles and mitigate conduct-related risks. In 2025, we introduced new Whistleblowing procedure and
Speak-up procedure. We continue to enforce international sanctions, prevent financial crime, and uphold zero tolerance for
bribery and corruption.

Our services remain focused on the Baltic region, and we maintain transparency through customer due diligence. While
politically neutral, we engage in industry associations to support responsible business practices. These ongoing efforts reflect
our dedication to integrity, accountability, and regulatory compliance.

Business model resilience
Business model resilience topic is not material for the current reporting period, and information is provided for context,
continuity and transparency purposes only. We continue to ensure the sustainability and adaptability of our business model
through our strategy, risk management and sustainability frameworks. Our three-year financial plan – developed across business
and risk functions, reviewed annually, and approved by the Council – is aligned with our risk appetite and financial targets,
including climate targets.

We manage business model risk by continuously evaluating market conditions, geopolitical developments, and performance.
ESG considerations are integrated into strategic planning through our DMAs and climate and environmental risk assessments.
For all material ESG-related risks and the related impacts, transition plans are established. Progress on strategy implementation
and transition plans is monitored via KPIs, with quarterly reviews by the management bodies. These efforts are supported by
dedicated operational resources and reflect our commitment to long-term resilience and responsible growth.

Cybersecurity
Cybersecurity topic is not material for the current reporting period, and information is provided for context, continuity and
transparency purposes only. We continue to implement our three-year cybersecurity strategy built around zero-tolerance for
critical incidents, zero-trust network architecture, and cloud-based defences. Our 24-hour Security Operations Centre is
supported by incident response playbooks and post-incident reviews. Third-party risks are managed through onboarding
assessments, contractual obligations, and periodic audits. To maintain security, we have invested in technologies– while
redundancy and backup systems ensure service continuity.

Our commitment to customer data protection includes independent Data Protection Officers, comprehensive training
programs, and ongoing GDPR compliance monitoring. Key performance indicators such as cybersecurity training completion
rates, incident detection and response times, and third-party security assessments are tracked and aligned with the NIST
Cybersecurity Framework and DORA regulations. In 2025, we refined our privacy and cybersecurity practices, expanded
resilience testing, and adapted to evolving legal interpretations of GDPR.

2.   Explanation of negative assessment
ESRS E2 POLLUTION
We have assessed a comprehensive list of IROs related to Pollution as part of the current Double Materiality Assessment (DMA)
and concluded that this topic is not material for Luminor. This conclusion is based on the application of ESRS materiality criteria
to the Luminor's actual and potential impacts, risks and opportunities.

The IROs assessed cover our own operations, our suppliers and customers, and risks of financing companies that contribute to
air and water pollution, including hazardous waste generation, chemical discharge, and eutrophication of the Baltic Sea; credit
risk from clients in high-pollution sectors such as mining, chemicals, and shipping; and opportunities to increase revenue by
financing pollution mitigation technologies and circular economy solutions. Pollution to air was assessed separately within DMA
and deemed non-material because CO₂ emissions are already addressed under the material topic of Climate Change, while
other air emissions (e.g., methane, nitrous oxide, fluorinated gases) were assessed as not giving rise to material impacts or
financial risks for Luminor, and are mitigated by customers operating under strict EU regulations, as well as requirement under
our ESG risk assessment process for high-risk clients to establish transition plans.

Certain subtopics were assessed and not identified as material, as they do not give rise to material impacts, risks or
opportunities in relation to Luminor’s business model. These include pollution of living organisms and food resources,
substances of concern, substances of very high concern, and microplastics. Luminor does not engage in activities introducing
persistent pollutants, and indirect exposures are managed through ESG risk screening and sustainable procurement standards,
making standalone assessments duplicative and non-decision-useful.

The bank operates within the Baltic region under robust EU regulatory frameworks governing chemical safety, water quality,
and pollution prevention. ESG credit screening, portfolio diversification, and governance practices further support the
mitigation of residual risks. Potential impacts and opportunities are indirect, gradual, and misaligned with Luminor’s core
portfolio, with no evidence of systemic incidents or financial effects exceeding materiality thresholds. Considering these factors,
pollution-related ESRS topics do not meet the criteria for materiality under the impact, risk, and opportunity perspective.

ESRS E3 WATER AND MARINE RESOURCES
Water and marine resource topics were assessed as part of the current DMA and concluded to be not material for Luminor.
This conclusion is based on the application of ESRS materiality criteria to the Luminor's actual and potential impacts, risks and
opportunities.

Our water use is limited to standard office and data centre needs, with negligible withdrawals and routine discharges managed
through municipal systems. We have no processes generating significant wastewater, no coastal facilities, and no interaction
with marine environments, making ocean discharges and marine resource extraction irrelevant based on the assessment of
related impacts, risks and opportunities.

Potential indirect exposure through financing clients in sectors with higher water or marine risks, such as agriculture or
aquaculture, were also assessed under the DMA. These exposures are limited to the Baltic region and subject to robust EU
regulatory frameworks, contributing to immateriality conclusion. Water stress in the Baltics is currently low and projected to
remain moderate in the short and medium term, while marine-based economic activity within the portfolio is minimal.
Opportunities to finance water-efficient technologies or sustainable marine practices exist but remain niche and misaligned
with strategic priorities. Considering the negligible direct impacts, constrained indirect exposures, and absence of systemic
incidents or financial effects exceeding materiality thresholds, ESRS E3 topics do not meet the criteria for materiality under the
impact, risk, and opportunity perspective.

ESRS S1 OWN WORKFORCE
Own workforce topics under ESRS S1 were assessed as part of the current DMA and concluded to be not material for Luminor.
This conclusion is based on the application of ESRS materiality criteria to the Luminor's actual and potential impacts, risks and
opportunities.




92     Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025

=== pdf p.93 ===
Subtopics such as secure employment, working time, adequate wages, health and safety, work-life balance, diversity, gender
equality, inclusion of persons with disabilities, training and skills development, and measures against workplace violence were
analysed in detail. While these areas are important for employee well-being, they are comprehensively addressed through
Luminor’s internal governance frameworks and Baltic labour laws, leaving no residual risk or variability. Existing practices, such
as competitive compensation, diversity programs, health and safety measures, and grievance mechanisms, are embedded in
operations and supported by monitoring tools. Given Luminor’s business model focused on retail and corporate banking,
workforce factors do not materially influence core financial drivers, and the likelihood of significant financial or societal impact
remains low.

Other work-related rights, including child labour, forced labour, adequate housing, and privacy were assessed under the DMA
and not identified as material, as they do not give rise to material impacts, risks or opportunities in relation to Luminor’s
operating model. All employees are verified against national minimum-age requirements during recruitment, labour laws
prohibit any form of forced work, and Luminor does not provide housing benefits. Privacy risks are managed through established
data protection governance and controls and are governed by strict EU and national data protection regulations. Considering
these conditions and the absence of systemic incidents or financial effects exceeding materiality thresholds, ESRS S1 topics do
not meet the criteria for materiality under the impact, risk, and opportunity perspective.

ESRS S2 WORKERS IN THE VALUE CHAIN
Workers in the value chain topics under ESRS S2 were assessed as part of the current DMA and concluded to be not material
for Luminor. This conclusion is based on the application of ESRS materiality criteria to the Luminor's actual and potential
impacts, risks and opportunities.

Subtopics such as secure employment, working time, adequate wages, health and safety, social dialogue, freedom of association,
collective bargaining, diversity, and work-life balance were analyzed. While these issues are important for fair labour practices,
Luminor’s value‑chain counterparties predominantly operate in sectors such as IT, consultancy, and administrative services
rather than high‑risk industries. As a result, the likelihood of systemic harm or significant financial impact related to these
subtopics was assessed as very low. Additionally, these are comprehensively regulated and enforced within the Baltic region.

Other work-related rights, including child labor, forced labor, adequate housing, and water and sanitation are not identified as
material. The nature of services provided by suppliers does not involve housing or sanitation arrangements, and no exposures
associated with these risks were identified. Our suppliers and vendors are subject to strict EU labor standards, any possible
indirect exposure is limited to the Baltic region and governed by robust regulatory frameworks. Considering these conditions
and the absence of identified incidents or financial effects exceeding materiality thresholds, ESRS S2 topics do not meet the
criteria for materiality under the impact, risk, and opportunity perspective.

ESRS S3 AFFECTED COMMUNITIES
The affected communities topics under ESRS S3 were assessed as part of the current DMA and concluded to be not material
for Luminor. This conclusion is based on the application of ESRS materiality criteria to the Luminor's actual and potential
impacts, risks and opportunities.

The analysis focused on security-related impacts and potential risks from financing large-scale infrastructure projects, which
could lead to displacement or degradation of living spaces. These risks are minimal given Luminor’s portfolio, which is
concentrated in mortgages, SME lending, and corporate banking in urban areas, with no strategic focus on rural development
or large-scale projects. Opportunities such as financing housing cooperatives or regional development were also considered
but remain niche and misaligned with Luminor’s core business model.

Other subtopics, including adequate housing, food, water and sanitation, land‑related impacts, civil and political rights, and the
rights of indigenous peoples, were assessed under the DMA and not identified as material. Luminor does not finance sectors
typically associated with these risks, nor does it operate in jurisdictions with indigenous communities or elevated systemic
human‑rights risks. Additionally, these are comprehensively safeguarded by strong legal and regulatory frameworks in the Baltic
region. Considering the negligible direct impacts, limited indirect exposure, and absence of systemic incidents or financial




                                                                                        Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025          93

=== pdf p.94 ===
effects exceeding materiality thresholds, ESRS S3 topics do not meet the criteria for materiality under the impact, risk, and
opportunity perspective.

ESRS G1 BUSINESS CONDUCT
Business conduct topics under ESRS G1 were assessed as part of the current DMA and concluded to be not material for Luminor.
This conclusion is based on the application of ESRS materiality criteria to the Luminor's actual and potential impacts, risks and
opportunities.

The analysis covered risks such as poor corporate culture affecting employee engagement, conflicts of interest in product
distribution, corruption and bribery, financial crime, insider information misuse, and regulatory compliance failures.
Opportunities related to positive supervisory outcomes and policy engagement were also considered. While these issues are
important for effective governance, they are managed through established internal policies, controls, and oversight mechanisms
embedded in day‑to‑day operations. Existing measures, including whistleblower channels, internal audits, compliance
monitoring, and risk‑culture programmes, contribute to the mitigation of identified risks. No evidence of systemic misconduct
or financial effects exceeding ESRS materiality thresholds was identified.

Animal welfare was assessed as not material because it is irrelevant to Luminor’s business model. As a financial services provider,
Luminor does not engage in activities involving animals, such as agriculture, research, or product development. Our operations
are limited to office and digital environments, with no direct or indirect impact on animal well-being. Considering these
conditions and strong regional legislation protecting animal rights, this topic is excluded from the full materiality analysis. Overall,
ESRS G1 topics do not meet the criteria for materiality under the impact, risk, and opportunity perspective.

ESRS BUSINESS MODEL RESILIENCE
Business model resilience was assessed as part of the current DMA and concluded to be not material for Luminor. This
conclusion is based on the application of ESRS materiality criteria to the Luminor's actual and potential impacts, risks and
opportunities.

The analysis considered risks such as inadequate management of capital adequacy and liquidity, which could undermine
financial stability; failure to ensure business continuity, potentially leading to layoffs or partner losses; market abuse risks,
including insider list management and personal transactions; and compliance breaches related to tax evasion or suspicious
supplier activities. Opportunities linked to positive supervisory outcomes and operational resilience were also reviewed. While
these aspects are critical for sound governance, they are managed through established internal frameworks and controls
embedded in day‑to‑day operations. Existing measures, including ICAAP and ILAAP processes, stress testing, liquidity
management, and compliance monitoring, contribute to the mitigation of identified risks. Additionally, they are comprehensively
addressed through EU prudential regulations. No evidence suggests systemic harm or financial effects exceeding ESRS
materiality thresholds.

Considering the strong regulatory environment, robust internal controls, and absence of identified incidents, business model
resilience does not meet the criteria for materiality under the impact, risk, and opportunity perspective.

ESRS CYBERSECURITY
Cybersecurity was assessed as part of the current DMA and concluded to be not material for Luminor. This conclusion is based
on the application of ESRS materiality criteria to the Luminor's actual and potential impacts, risks and opportunities. The analysis
considered risks such as data breaches, financial network disruptions, and inadequate cybersecurity arrangements that could
lead to financial losses, erosion of customer trust, or service interruptions. Potential escalation of cyber-warfare was also
reviewed. While these risks are internally significant for operational resilience, they do not meet ESRS materiality thresholds for
external reporting because impacts are contained through robust governance and technical controls. Luminor’s cybersecurity
framework is aligned with EU regulations and industry best practices, supported by ongoing risk assessments, resilience
planning, and structured incident management processes to ensure service continuity and data protection. Considering the
strong regulatory environment, comprehensive internal controls, and absence of systemic incidents or financial effects
exceeding materiality thresholds, cybersecurity does not meet the criteria for materiality under the impact, risk, and
opportunity perspective.

4.      Our Policies, Procedures, and Standards
Internal regulation                          Description of key contents

Adverse Media Screening Instruction          This instruction defines the process of screening for adverse media information in public sources and describes the roles and
                                             responsibilities in investigating the risks identified during the process. The purpose of adverse media screening is to prevent Luminor being
                                             used for financial crime and engaging with legal entities or private individuals who are involved in or related to or found guilty of financial
                                             crime or ESG related offences. Daily exposure checks for high risk clients against adverse media let us identify existing or perspective
                                             customers that might be victims or perpetrators or accomplices of financial crime.
Business Model Risk Policy                   This policy sets out the core components of business model risk management, including Group Strategy, Financial Plan, products & pricing
                                             framework, performance criteria, and performance management, as well as related principles and limitations. The regulation outlines how
                                             potential key vulnerabilities to our business model arising from identified ESG risk drivers should be considered during the Group Strategy
                                             planning process, and product & pricing framework development.
Code of Conduct (the Code)                   This is an annex to our Code of Conduct which outlines our values and principles for responsible business conduct that we expect third
                                             parties to follow, including concerns for the impact on society and the environment of the business activities. We supplement this annex to
                                             our agreements with all suppliers and vendors from outside the EU/EEA unless they confirm that their own approved internal regulations are
                                             aligned with our conduct principles.
Code of Responsible Business Conduct for     This is an annex to our Code of Conduct which outlines our values and principles for responsible business conduct that we expect third
Third Parties                                parties to follow, including concerns for the impact on society and the environment of business activities. We supplement this annex to our
                                             agreements with all suppliers and vendors from outside the EU/EEA unless they confirm that their own approved internal regulations are
                                             aligned with our conduct principles.

Compliance Risk Policy                       Compliance Risk Policy outlines essential components for robust Compliance Risk management. It defines principles for integrating external
                                             requirements into internal control systems and governance arrangements.
Conflict of Interest Management Standard &   The internal regulations sets the requirements for identifying, preventing and managing the Conflicts of Interest in Luminor. Conflicts of
Conflict of Interest Management Procedure    Interest can be related to Employees, Management Bodies, structural units, third parties, business activities, including the provision of loans,
                                             the provision of Investment and / or Ancillary Services, the provision of Pension Fund management services, launch of a new product or
                                             service, approval of a new target market, a change to an existing product or service or the defined target market, or ad hoc review.

Customer Complaints, Feedback and            The internal regulations together set forth the framework and overall principles for handling of customer complaints, feedback and requests,
Requests Handling Procedure (& also          as well as mistakes found by our employees. They outline roles and responsibilities of structural units in complaints handling, reporting,
Standard)                                    analyzing data and following-up on improvements. When mitigating negative impacts, we follow the applicable EU and national regulations.
                                             These provisions also apply i to our external vendors acting under an agreement to sell our products, and to all the customer segments we
                                             serve, including third party service providers who use our open banking solutions.

Being Human – Luminor guide to a             The standard outlines the essential guidelines and best practice for delivering exceptional customer service. It aims to enhance customer
memorable customer experience                satisfaction and loyalty through consistency, efficiency and high-quality interactions across all customer touchpoints. It sets out detailed
                                             steps for handling customer inquiries, resolving issues, and maintaining a positive customer experience.

Data Protection Standard                     This standard establishes the requirements for the protection and handling of personal data. It defines the organizational roles and
                                             responsibilities for addressing the specific compliance obligations arising from data protection laws and regulations, including but not limited
                                             to the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Furthermore, these standard outlines the process for monitoring and controlling
                                             adherence to both this internal regulation and applicable external data protection requirements.
Data Quality Management Procedure            The regulation defines the main principles and responsibilities for data quality management, setting out guidelines for data collection,
                                             storage, architecture, and aggregation, and for monitoring of data quality for the completeness, validity, timeliness, accuracy, consistency
                                             and uniqueness of the data, as well as remediation steps for if data quality issues arise. It aims to establish a standardised and systematic
                                             approach to evaluating and improving the quality of data across the organisation. This approach is designed to follow the principles outlined
                                             in the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Standard no. 239.
Data Specification for ESG Data Proxies      This internal regulation describes all of the data requirements needed for developing the ESG risk data model, including the data sources,
                                             and where to get the data needed. This internal regulation also provides the methodologies for estimating the data attributes if the data are
                                             not yet in our systems or if it is not possible to get the data needed in the right format from external data providers.

Discretionary Portfolio Management ESG       The procedure sets out how ESG risks and principal adverse impacts are integrated in the investment decision making processes, following
Due Diligence Procedure                      the principles set in our Sustainability Policy and the Sustainable Investment Guidelines, when managing client investment portfolio on a
                                             discretionary basis. It outlines how the ESG due diligence assessment is performed before and during the investment decision making
                                             process, including the relevant methodology and the allocation of responsibility when the principal adverse impact prioritisation framework
                                             is applied. The regulation also defines roles and responsibilities for monitoring and reporting processes.
Double Materiality Assessment Procedure      The procedure defines the Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) processes for identification, assessment, management, and disclosure of
                                             sustainability-related impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs), as well as risk treatment approaches through a dedicated DMA Outcome
                                             Memo. Material Sustainability Matters are identified and assessed from both impact and financial materiality perspectives, relying on
                                             stakeholder engagement. The DMA outcomes are reviewed and approved by the Management Board, overseen by Supervisory Council, and
                                             the outcome are integrated into Luminor's business strategy, risk management processes and sustainability reporting in accordance with the
                                             Sustainability Reporting Standard. The procedure aligns with the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) and Sustainability
                                             Accounting Standards Board (SASB) Standards.
ESG Data Management Procedure                This procedure establishes the principles, roles, and responsibilities for managing ESG data within Luminor in line with our data management
                                             framework. It aims to ensure accurate and reliable ESG data management to support informed decision-making and compliance with
                                             internal and external reporting requirements. The procedure details the process of collaboration between business units and support
                                             functions, covering stages from initiation and analysis to implementation and finalization. Regular monitoring and documentation are in place
                                             to maintain data quality and integrity.

=== pdf p.104 ===
Internal regulation                           Description of key contents

ESG Due Diligence Standard                    This document establishes our principles, roles and responsibilities, and describes the steps to be followed when the ESG Due Diligence
                                              process is applied in our business activities, decision making and relationships with our employees, customers, vendors, and suppliers. The
                                              aim is to avoid or minimise any harm to society and the environment that might be caused by our business activities or those of our
                                              customers, vendors and suppliers. This standard has been developed in accordance with the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible
                                              Business Conduct and builds on the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, the UN Sustainable Development Goals, the EBRD
                                              Environmental and Social Risk Categorisation List, the EU Taxonomy, and other relevant EU regulations. The standard is aligned with the
                                              Luminor Risk Policy and Strategy for the non-financial risk assessment grid and with the Sustainability Policy for the exclusion list from our
                                              direct investments and financing universe.

ESG Risk Assessment Procedure                 This internal regulation defines ESG Risk assessment principles for legal entities which is a part of the overall creditworthiness assessment
                                              process. The procedure establishes a risk-based approach for ESG risk assessment process, focusing on customers whose inherent
                                              environmental, social and governance risks are high and the size of their credit exposure is material to the Luminor. An enhanced risk
                                              assessment is performed for the customers where elevated inherent ESG risks are identified, conclusions on the customer's risk mitigation
                                              capacity are drawn and the residual risk level is defined. Main conclusions and the residual ESG risk level are documented and considered in
                                              the credit decision making process.

Individual Performance Management             The procedure outlines the process for managing individual performance within the Luminor Group, setting out the roles and responsibilities
Procedure                                     of managers and employees. It describes how to set individual goals, provide regular feedback through one-to-one meetings and quarterly
                                              snaps, and conduct year-end reviews. The procedure aims to create clarity, build alignment, and develop the abilities needed for executing
                                              the strategy. It also addresses how to manage poor performance through informal counselling and formal improvement plans, and to ensure
                                              that employees are given opportunities to improve and are supported in their development.
Industry ESG Risk Management Procedure        This is a subordinated document to the ESG Risk Assessment Procedure that provides additional guidance for sectors with medium or high
                                              climate risk exposure. It details sector-specific climate risks and risk drivers, and outlines possible ways of mitigating risks, such as
                                              developing climate-friendly policies and procedures, setting targets and metrics, and main elements of transition planning. It also describes
                                              the general lending guidance as defined in ESG Risk Assessment Procedure and expectations for customers in these sectors towards
                                              mitigating and adapting to climate change, pursuing energy efficiency, shifting towards increased use of renewable energy, etc.

Lending Risk Parameters for Private           This internal regulation describes the main lending criteria and conditions that are applicable to private lending, including leasing. The
Individuals Procedure                         document covers loan participants, main loan features, applicable risk ratios, and main characteristics of the real estate pledge.
Performance Management Procedure              The procedure provides a structured and systematic approach to managing the Luminor Group’s performance in alignment with the Strategy
                                              and the Financial Plan of the organization. It outlines main rules and principles used for performance management and sets out roles and
                                              responsibilities applicable for the performance management process, which includes KPI setting for Senior Management, monitoring
                                              progress against strategic and financial targets, and conducting regular follow-ups to ensure effective strategy execution.

Procedure for Personal Transactions in        This Procedure implements the Personal Transaction requirements applicable to the employees of investment firms as set forth in the MiFID
Financial Instruments                         II Regulation on Organisational Requirements, the related requirements stemming from the Market Abuse Regulation and requirements
                                              applicable to the Personal Transactions of Employees of Asset Management Companies. The Procedure supports implementation of the
                                              Compliance Risk Policy and Compliance Standards by providing detailed guidance on the specific steps to be taken and by defining the
                                              respective roles and responsibilities

Procedure of Handling of Inside Information   This Procedure sets out the principles and measures that Luminor takes to ensure due handling and disclosure of Inside Information in order
and Insider List                              to prevent market abuse activities in conformity with the requirements of the Market Abuse Regulation and its underlying regulations. The
                                              Procedure supports implementation of the Compliance Risk Policy and the Compliance Standards with a detailed guidance on specific
                                              preventive actions to be taken and a definition of the respective roles and responsibilities of the Employees.
Product Management Procedure                  This procedure governs the processes for managing Luminor's products, including developing new products, making changes to existing
                                              products, and decommissioning. It establishes the definitions of products and provides guidelines for product documentation and
                                              assessment processes. We aim to ensure that our customer interests, objectives, characteristics, and sustainability preferences are
                                              considered, potential consumer detriment is mitigated, and conflicts of interest are minimized. The procedure aligns product management
                                              with Luminor's business strategy, and our internal regulations for risk management and accounting.

Remuneration Policy                           The policy is designed to produce transparent and balanced remuneration programmes that align individual performance with the long-term
                                              goals of the organisation. The aim is to attract, develop, and retain motivated and skilled employees without encouraging excessive risk-
                                              taking. The policy emphasises equal opportunities and non-discrimination within both fixed and variable remuneration, and it contains
                                              measures for preventing mis-selling in retail banking and ensuring fairness in investment services. The remuneration structure has fixed and
                                              variable components, with performance fees at the discretion of the Supervisory Council, and with priority given to financial stability and
                                              regulatory compliance.

Risk Appetite Statement (RAS)                 The Statement is a strategic document and a deliverable that is governed by the Risk Policy and prepared in accordance with the Risk
                                              Appetite Framework – Policy. The RAS defines the overall risk appetite, risk strategy, risk appetite statements, and metrics for all material
                                              Level 1 risk types that we are exposed to, and also for the risk drivers, which may influence a broad range of risk types and sub-types in a
                                              material way.

Risk Policy                                   The Risk Policy defines the risk management framework, the key risk management principles, and the roles and responsibilities for risk
                                              management within Luminor.
Sourcing and Third Party Management           This procedure establishes a consistent approach for the sourcing and purchasing of all goods and services and for managing the risks and
Procedure                                     performance-related activities throughout the third party management lifecycle: from the point when the business identifies that it needs to
                                              use a third party or intragroup service provider, up to when the agreement is renewed or terminated, or expires. It provides a set of
                                              templates for supplier due diligence questionnaires, depending on supplier classification, which all contain an ESG related questionnaire, and
                                              outlines their application process. The Procedure is aligned with the relevant guidelines of EBA and ESMA, and the EU Digital Operational
                                              Resilience Act.
Speak-Up Procedure                            This Procedure describes how submitted Speak-up Reports are received, assessed, recorded, and performed in a structured and respectful
                                              manner, safeguarding the rights of all parties involved and ensuring that any substantiated risks or issues are addressed appropriately. The
                                              speak-up process establishes reporting channels where a Reporter can submit their Speak-up Report. If a submitted Speak-up Report
                                              meets the requirements of whistleblowing, the Report is reviewed in accordance with the Whistleblowing Procedure.
Strategy Planning Procedure                   This procedure outlines the strategic planning process, which includes formulating and planning the execution of the long-term group
                                              strategy. This procedure encompasses the preparation, review and approval of the strategy, and planning for its execution, detailing the roles
                                              and responsibilities, the scope and structure of it, the annual cycle, and the approval process.

Internal regulation                     Description of key contents

Sustainability Policy                   This policy establishes the guiding principles and key components of the sustainability framework to be implemented in relevant Luminor
                                        business activities, decision‑making processes and relationships with our stakeholders to achieve our sustainability objectives. The policy
                                        outlines governance and responsibilities for the Supervisory Council and the Management Board and prescribes the integration of ESG
                                        aspects into strategy, risk management, transition planning, and reporting. Our policy follows the guidance from international standards
                                        including the UN Sustainable Development Goals, the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, the UN Global Compact, the
                                        OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Business Conduct, the International
                                        Labour Organization (ILO) Conventions, the Paris Agreement, and the Kunming‑Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

Sustainability Reporting Standard       The standard outlines the process, roles, and principles for preparing Luminor's annual and quarterly sustainability disclosures. The objective
                                        is to ensure accurate, fair, comprehensive, balanced, and timely disclosure of sustainability-related information. The process involves
                                        gathering information, validating and signing off disclosures, and obtaining approval from the Management Board and Supervisory Council.
                                        The disclosures are integrated into the Management Report and aligned with the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS),
                                        Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), and other relevant regulations.
Sustainable Investment Due Diligence    This procedure describes how ESG risks and adverse sustainability impacts are integrated into the investment decision making processes for
Procedure of Luminor Asset Management   Luminor Asset Management Subsidiaries. Following the SFDR provisions, our Sustainability Policy and the Sustainable Investment Guidelines,
and Pension Companies                   the procedure establishes different types of financial instruments with regards to their sustainability characteristics and sets out how the
                                        ESG due diligence assessment is executed for the financial instruments proposed for the pension funds. The regulation also defines roles
                                        and responsibilities for monitoring and reporting processes on sustainability-related disclosures.

Sustainable Investment Guidelines       The guidelines outline sustainable investment principles, including the ESG risk integration in the investment decision making process in
                                        Luminor Bank and its Asset Management Subsidiaries. The guidelines apply to direct and indirect investments in the provision of
                                        discretionary portfolio management services, management of pension funds, pension plans and pension schemes, and investment on our
                                        own account through Luminor liquidity bond portfolio management, and bond trading. The sustainable investment guidelines were
                                        developed in accordance with the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR), the United Nations Principles for Responsible
                                        Investment (UN PRI), the EU Action Plan for Financing Sustainable Growth, and other applicable legal acts.

Third Party Risk Management Standard    This Standard provides the principles for managing Third Party Risk across end-to-end Third Party Risk management lifecycle. It sets out the
                                        minimum principles for sourcing process, requirements for identifying critical agreements with third parties, including intragroup service
                                        providers, assigning roles and responsibilities across Three Lines, and overseeing management, monitoring, and governance of Third Party
                                        agreements and their risks. This Standard also defines reporting obligations within Luminor and to relevant regulatory bodies, as well as the
                                        escalation process for Third Party agreement related risks and events. The Standard is aligned with the relevant guidelines of EBA and ESMA,
                                        and the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act.

Whistleblowing Procedure                This Procedure ensures secure, clear and consistent process for reporting, investigating Whistleblowing Reports within Luminor, ensuring
                                        compliance with the EU and national laws and regulations, and protection for Whistleblowers against retaliation.

8.    Subsequent events
In January 2026, we approved the new Sustainability Standard and updated ESG Risk Assessment Procedure integrating the
customer engagement approach and biodiversity and nature services degradation related questions for high-risk agriculture
customers into the related due diligence tooling.

In February 2026, we approved the risk mitigation approach and transition plans for Luminor ESG-related material risks and the
related impacts that were deemed material in scope of 2025 Double Materiality Assessment process, including the C&E
Transition plan. In February 2026, we completed the climate and environmental risk stress testing process.

NOTES TO THE CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
1.    Material accounting policy information
Luminor Bank AS (which, together with its subsidiaries, is referred to as ‘Luminor’, below) is a credit institution with its
headquarters in Tallinn. Luminor is owned by Luminor Holding (which is controlled ultimately by BCP VII, an investment fund
managed by an affiliate of Blackstone) which, in turn, is owned by a consortium led by private equity funds managed by
Blackstone (80.05%) and DNB Bank (19.95%). These consolidated financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2025,
which have been prepared on a going concern basis, were approved by the Management Board on 24 March, the Supervisory
Council on 26 March, and by the shareholder on 26 March 2026.

BASIS OF PRESENTATION
The Consolidated financial statements (the Statements) of Luminor are prepared in accordance with International Financial
Reporting Standards (the Standards) as endorsed by the European Union. In addition, Luminor has adopted the EU carve-out
version of IAS 39 to hedge the interest rate risk on a portfolio of non-maturing core deposits. The Statements are prepared
under the historical cost convention, except for financial instruments measured at fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL) or
other comprehensive income (FVTOCI), as well as financial assets and liabilities designated as hedged items in qualifying fair
value hedging relationships which are measured at amortised cost with adjustments for hedging gain or loss. In the primary
financial statements of Luminor as a separate entity which are disclosed in these Statements (Note 32, below), the investments
in subsidiaries are carried at cost less impairment.

The material accounting policy information and significant accounting estimates and judgements applied in the preparation of
these Statements are set out below. Luminor’s functional and presentation currency is the euro (EUR) and, unless otherwise
stated, all amounts are reported in millions of euros to one decimal place. Monetary assets and liabilities denominated in foreign
currencies are translated into euro at the official rate of the European Central Bank at the reporting period end.

Certain new Standards, amendments and interpretations to existing Standards, came into effect for accounting periods
beginning after 1 January 2025 or later periods. Amendments to Standards which became effective for annual periods beginning
on or after 1 January 2025, include amendments to IAS 1, IFRS 16, IAS 7, IAS 21 and IFRS 7. The impact of applying these changes
is not material. The International Accounting Standards Board has issued amendments to existing international accounting
standards (IAS 7, IAS 21, IFRS 7, IFRS 9 and IFRS 10) and new standard IFRS 19 that have not yet come into force. None of the
amendments is expected to have a significant impact on Luminor’s financial statements. There will be impact on the structure
and disclosures of the Statements from the implementation of the new standard IFRS 18 (effective as of 1 January 2027),
significance of which is currently being analysed.

FEE AND COMMISSION INCOME AND EXPENSE
Fees and commission income is recognised either over time as the services are rendered, when the customer simultaneously
receives and consumes the benefits provided by Luminor’s performance, or at a point in time when Luminor satisfies its
performance obligation, usually upon execution of the underlying transaction. The amount of fee or commission received, or
receivable, represents the transaction price for the services identified as distinct performance obligations.

Fees and commission recognised over time include fees for account maintenance, servicing, and subscription, portfolio and
other asset management advisory and services, wealth management and financial planning services, or fees for servicing loans
on behalf of third parties (except for those subject to effective interest rate). Variable fees are recognised only to the extent
that Management determines that it is highly probable that a significant reversal will not occur. Fees and commission recognised
at a point in time include fees for arranging a sale or purchase of foreign currencies on behalf of a customer, processing payment
transactions, cash settlements, collection or cash disbursements, and other commissions. Fee and commission expense is
recognised as the service is being received (accrual basis) and when liability has been incurred.

TEMPORARY BANK TAXES
Effective January 2024 the Government of Latvia enacted a temporary tax on credit providers as an amendment to the Latvian
‘Consumer Rights Protection Law’. This tax was levied on credit providers at a rate of 2% per annum of their total mortgage
loan portfolio as at 31 October 2023. The tax, which is payable at a rate of 0.5% per quarter, remained in force through 2024.

In 2024, Latvia enacted a second temporary bank tax, to be levied for three years starting in 2025 at a rate of 60% on the net
interest income that exceeds the average annual net interest income for the financial years 2018-2022 by more than 50%. The
amount of taxable income may be reduced if a certain rate of credit growth is attained. Lithuania extended until December
2025 a temporary tax introduced in 2023 on the selected income of banks earned within its jurisdiction. The tax is levied at a
rate of 60% on the net interest income generated in each of the years 2023, 2024, and 2025 from loans that were issued to
customers before 31 December 2022, if the net interest income generated exceeds the average net interest income of the
preceding four financial years by more than 50%. The expenses on both taxes are accounted for according to IAS 37/ IFRIC 21.

CASH AND BALANCES WITH CENTRAL BANKS
In the Statements of cash flows, cash and cash equivalents comprise cash balances, non-restricted balances due from the
central banks, and amounts due from other credit institutions with original maturity of less than 3 months and insignificant risk
due to change in value but excludes mandatory cash balances with central banks, which represent non-interest-bearing
mandatory reserve deposits which are not available to finance Luminor’s day to day operations.

SYNTHETIC SECURITISATION
Loans subject to synthetic securitisation remain on balance sheet, with credit protection realised through purchase of
guarantees. Any impairment allowances for expected credit losses are calculated without consideration of the guarantee
protection bought. The reimbursement right under the guarantees are recognized as an asset and reflected in net other finance
income once it is virtually certain that the reimbursement amount for qualifying losses will be received. The related guarantee
fees are accounted as other administrative expenses.

TANGIBLE AND INTANGIBLE ASSETS, LESSEE CONTRACTS ACCOUNTING
Tangible assets are recorded at cost minus accumulated depreciation and impairment losses. Equipment is depreciated
between 20 and 33% per annum, and property between 1% and 2% per annum. For property leases Luminor uses its own funding
cost as a discount rate. For other assets Luminor uses the interest rate implicit in the lease. Payments associated with leases
with a 12-month term or less, or with a value of less than 5,000 EUR, are recognized on a straight-line basis as an expense in
profit or loss. Intangible assets are carried at cost minus accumulated amortisation and impairment losses and amortised over
3 to 5 years.

IMPAIRMENT OF GOODWILL
Luminor tests whether goodwill has suffered any impairment at least annually or more frequently if indications of impairment
exist. For 2024 and 2025, the recoverable amount of the cash-generating units was determined based on value-in-use
calculations which require the use of assumptions. The calculations use discounted cash flow method covering the period of
ten years. Beyond ten-years projections are made using estimated industry growth rates relevant to the cash-generating unit.

HEDGE ACCOUNTING
At the inception of a hedge relationship, Luminor formally designates and documents the hedge relationship to which it wishes
to apply hedge accounting and the risk management objective and strategy for undertaking the hedge. The documentation
includes identification of the hedging instrument, the hedged item, the nature of the risk being hedged and how Luminor will
assess whether the hedging relationship meets the hedge effectiveness requirements (including the analysis of sources of hedge
ineffectiveness and how the hedge ratio is determined).

A hedging relationship qualifies for hedge accounting if it meets all of the following effectiveness requirements: there is ‘an
economic relationship’ between the hedged item and the hedging instrument; the effect of credit risk does not ‘dominate the
value changes’ that resulting from that economic relationship; the hedge ratio of the hedging relationship is the same as that
resulting from the quantity of the hedged item that Luminor actually hedges and the quantity of the hedging instrument that
Luminor actually uses to hedge that quantity of the hedged item.




                                                                                      Luminor Bank Annual Report 2025         121

=== pdf p.122 ===
Luminor applies hedge accounting according to IFRS 9 Financial instruments to fair value hedges of euro-denominated senior
preferred and covered bond Debt securities issue, and to part of Deposits from customers according to EU carve-out version
of IAS 39. Luminor enters into interest rate swaps to hedge its Debt securities issued and part of deposit portfolio and applies
a fair value hedge. Changes in the fair value are presented under "Net gain (-loss) from financial instruments at fair value" in the
Statement of Profit or Loss. Interest income and expense from financial instruments (hedged item) are presented as “Net
interest and similar income”. The changes in the fair value of the hedged Debt securities issued attributable to the hedged risk
are recognised as an addition to or deduction from the balance sheet value of financial liabilities and presented under "Net gain
(-loss) on financial instruments at fair value" in the income statement.

The carrying amount of the derivatives used to hedge Deposits from customers are included in line item ‘Derivatives’ in the
Statement of Financial Position, on either the Assets or Liabilities side depending on the fair value of the instruments, whereas
portfolio hedging effect is recognised as ‘Fair value of changes of hedged items in hedges of interest rate’ in the Statement of
Financial Position, on Liabilities side corresponding to the change in fair value of designated customer deposits discounted at
market interest rates.

CORPORATE INCOME TAX
Quarterly profits of credit institutions in Estonia are subject to advance corporate income tax at a rate of 18% (previously 14%).
The profit of a quarter can be reduced by losses of up to 19 previous quarters. Quarterly advance corporate income tax
payments can be offset by the corporate income tax liability, charged at a rate of 22% arising from profit distribution. If no
dividends are paid, the quarterly advance corporate income tax payments are not refunded. Corporate income tax payable on
the quarterly profits is recognised as a current income tax expense. Deferred tax asset (and deferred tax income) on quarterly
losses is recognised only if it is probable that future taxable profits will be available during 19 subsequent quarters to utilise
those losses. The corporate income tax arising from the payment of dividends is accounted for as an expense in the period
when dividends are declared, regardless of the actual payment date or the period for which the dividends are paid.

Since 2024, Latvia introduced annual mandatory prepayment of corporate income tax for credit institutions and consumer
credit service providers, at a rate of 20% on prior year after-tax profit. Payments were reduced by the amount of tax paid on
profits already distributed in the tax year. Accruals for mandatory prepayment of corporate income tax were created in 2025.
Prior 2024 in Latvia, corporate income tax was charged upon distribution of profits or conditionally distributed profit at the rate
of 20% of the gross amount. Corporate income tax on distributed profit was recognised when the shareholders of Luminor
decided on profit distribution. Corporate income tax was recognised as expenses in the profit and loss calculation in the
reporting period when the dividends or conditional dividends were calculated, whereas for other objects of conditionally
distributed profit corporate income tax was recognised at the moment when the expenses occurred within the reporting period.

In Lithuania the standard corporate income tax rate is 15%. For profits of credit institutions in excess of 2 million EUR the income
tax rate is 20%. Expenses related to taxation charges and included within these financial statements are based on calculations
made by Luminor in accordance with the Lithuanian tax legislation.

ISSUED DEBT AND EQUITY INSTRUMENTS
Luminor issues financial instruments either classified as a financial liability or equity. Issued financial instruments are classified
as financial liabilities if the contractual arrangements result in having a present obligation to either deliver cash or another
financial asset or a variable number of equity instruments to the holder of the instrument. If this is not the case, the instrument
is generally an equity instrument and classified as equity, net of transaction costs.

In February 2025 Luminor issued an Additional Tier 1 (AT1) Temporary Write Down Notes (perpetual subordinated instrument)
which will be written down temporarily in case a pre-defined CET1 trigger level is breached. Interest payments are fully
discretionary and mandatorily cancelled in certain circumstances. These instruments are classified as equity in accordance with
IAS 32 as there is no requirement for Luminor to pay interest or principal to the noteholders. AT1 instruments are initially
recognised at the fair value of proceeds received, net of directly attributable transaction costs, which are deducted from equity.
These instruments are not subsequently remeasured. Distributions on AT1 instruments are recognized directly in equity when
declared. Cancellation of distributions does not create a liability or result in a profit or loss impact.
